nytimes.com.title: The Man City Scandal Is About More Than Football
nytimes.com.text:
Manchester City first came to my attention after we moved from Berlin to Cardiff and my then-8-year-old son, an avid football fan, declared that Man City was now his team. It was 2024, and the club had just won its fourth consecutive Premier League title — unheard of. That was clearly enough for my Welsh son to set aside any misgivings he might have had about supporting an English club.
Those titles don’t look so shiny now. Last month, an independent commission found Man City had broken more than 100 of the league’s financial rules. It said the team, whose majority owner is Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the vice president of the United Arab Emirates, spent hundreds of millions of pounds it wasn’t allowed to spend, on players it could never have otherwise afforded. (Man City is appealing the ruling.)
I spoke to my colleague Tariq Panja, our global sports correspondent, about the biggest financial scandal in football history.
So Tariq, let’s talk about the scandal at Man City. Full disclosure: My 10-year-old is a Man City fan.
He’s not the only one! Kids love a winning team, and this generation of kids only know Man City as a winning team. But historically this was Manchester’s second team. It really wasn’t known for any great success — until Sept. 1, 2008. That’s the day Sheikh Mansour bought the club.

nytimes.com.title: A Rural Village Voted to Leave the U.K., Stirring Britain’s Migration Debate
nytimes.com.text:
“What a week we’ve had,” a triumphant Tim McNally told dozens of his neighbors in Piddington’s village hall.
“I said to you guys, we are going to turn Piddington, this small village, into the largest village on this earth,” Mr. McNally, the chair of the parish council, said on a Tuesday night in late September. “That we are going to put it on the map.”
And they had.
The village of just over 350 people voted on Sept. 15 to become independent of the United Kingdom, in protest against a government plan to house 1,250 male asylum seekers in a nearby former military site.
Piddington has not, in fact, broken away from the United Kingdom, as the referendum had no legal basis. But it catapulted the rural village in Oxfordshire to the top of news sites and social media feeds, a publicity coup that Mr. McNally likened to a “blueprint” for other places facing the possible arrival of asylum seekers.
Piddington swiftly became an example of how a small place could challenge a national government over concerns that inhabitants felt were being ignored. In this case, how could a small village with no shops or pubs cope with more than a thousand unemployed men suddenly on its outskirts?
The campaign, which at times amplified far-right talking points about immigrants, also illustrated how divisive migration has become around Europe. In Britain, while asylum applications are down since a peak late last year, they remain consistently higher than the pre-2021 average.

nytimes.com.title: The Wave of Student Protests Roiling France
nytimes.com.text:
Protests by high school students have rattled France in recent weeks, with hundreds of school blockages, large demonstrations and violent clashes with the police.
The students are protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and decrepit buildings. The French government is scrambling to address their frustrations, which erupted amid a heated political climate ahead of a presidential election in April and have threatened to swell into a broader wave of grievances.
More than 700 police officers and more than 300 students and school staff members have been injured, some of them seriously, according to the government. Some high schools were set on fire or ransacked, and hundreds more were damaged, according to the education ministry.
The government has tried to assuage students’ anger, in part by pledging to create emergency plans to address school staffing shortages. But deteriorating public finances have left officials without much wiggle room to address the students’ complaints, and concessions have done little to calm the protesters.

nytimes.com.title: Spain’s Protesters See ‘Madness’ of Rising Rent and a ‘Martyr’ in Maricarmen
nytimes.com.text:
Thousands of people marched in Madrid on Thursday in memory of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose dramatic eviction two weeks ago shook the country and prompted Spain’s left-wing prime minister to call snap elections over a housing crisis.
Before her death on Wednesday, Ms. Abascal, popularly known as Maricarmen, became a symbol of the housing crisis. Only about 20 percent of Spaniards have to rent their homes, but that share has increased in recent years as homeownership — deeply ingrained in Spain’s culture — slides further out of reach.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has portrayed his decision to hold elections as a chance for his left-wing bloc to get a majority in Parliament that would tackle the housing crisis. But it remains far from clear whether the issue will sway enough voters, as conservative and far-right parties frame the election as a referendum on Mr. Sánchez himself.
And as the parties wrangle, many Spaniards are staying in the streets, saying they feel crushed by the problems of rising rent and stagnant wages.
Nationally, rents have risen 87 percent since 2015, while salaries have climbed only 28 percent, according to an analysis by the newspaper El País. As a result, many young Spaniards stay in their parents’ homes well into their 30s. Newly arrived migrants pack into small apartments with other families. And many longtime residents are forced to leave their neighborhoods as their rents jump.
I spoke with dozens of protesters on Thursday evening about why they had joined the march, their own housing situations and what Ms. Abascal meant to them.

nytimes.com.title: U.N. Warns Against Technology Used to Read Citizens’ Minds
nytimes.com.text:
The scenarios sound like science fiction: Police officers accessing data contained in suspects’ brains to forcefully extract information, or to predict if offenders might plan to commit future crimes.
But the secretary-general of the United Nations warned on Thursday for the first time that neurotechnologies are advancing so rapidly that governments’ ability to access and manipulate people’s brains could one day pose a threat to fundamental human rights.
The abuse of future technologies, Secretary-General António Guterres warned, could lead to arbitrary detentions, the alteration of people’s mental states and infringements on privacy.
“Neurotechnology, including new and emerging forms, raises profound human rights challenges when applied to the administration of justice,” the secretary-general wrote. “Its expansion beyond clinical settings into investigative, judicial and correctional contexts introduces significant risks, alongside potential benefits.”
Human rights officials said the document was an important step toward raising global awareness of the issue and that it could help countries develop laws to prevent the abuse of such technology.

cnn.com.title: One of the world’s wealthiest cities is enduring the world’s most polluted air. Here’s why
cnn.com.text: Singapore, one of the wealthiest cities in the world, has become the most polluted on the planet as it chokes under a blanket of thick, toxic smog caused by fires in neighboring Indonesia. Pollution has cast a pall on the city-state as it gets ready to host a packed weekend of marquee events ranging from international conferences to the glitzy Formula One Grand Prix night race. Air quality in the city-state was at the “very unhealthy” range with an air quality index (AQI) of 216 Friday mid-morning, according to Swiss air quality monitor IQAir. The financial hub topped the list of most polluted cities by IQAir this week and was still at the top spot Friday morning. Kuala Lumpur, also deeply affected by the Indonesian fires, was at number two. Singapore’s skyline, including Marina Bay Sands and other skyscrapers were reduced to faint silhouettes amid the pollution. The key Asian financial hub – with a population of 6.21 million and annual GDP of more than $650 billion – and neighboring Malaysia have had to endure the haze almost annually. Fires in Indonesia are an annual event during the country’s dry season when huge stretches of peatland are cleared and drained for commercial plantations, including those that produce palm oil, an ingredient used in a slew of products from noodles to toothpaste. But this year, the arrival of what’s expected to be a “super” El Niño — a supercharged version of the natural climate pattern which tends to bring bone dry conditions to the country — has set the stage for unusually intense blazes. In an update on its website Thursday, Singapore’s National Environment Agency said “moderate to dense smoke plumes from southern and central Sumatra and West Kalimantan were observed to drift towards Singapore,” referring to Indonesian regions. “Under the prevailing southeasterly or southerly winds, smoke haze may continue to drift towards Singapore,” it added. Entertainment events held outdoors at the F1 event in Singapore could potentially be affected but not the race itself, the motorsport’s governing FIA said Thursday, according to Reuters. On Friday, race organizer Singapore GP told CNN “there are currently no plans to modify our entertainment activities” at the event. Acts to entertain F1 spectators include Janet Jackson and The Killers, among others. This is not the first time the Singapore night race is facing air quality issues. The races in 2015 and 2019 were also enveloped in thick haze and they went ahead. Nevertheless, the Singapore Tourism Board told CNN on Friday: “Action plans are in place based on the intensity of the haze.” F1 drivers, however, don’t seem too bothered. Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas, who cycled more than 400km (248 miles) from Malaysia to Singapore this week, told Reuters: “I don’t feel like it’s that extreme yet. I mean, it’s not great, but I don’t think there’s that much you can do.” Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton told Reuters he has “much bigger issues to focus on.” Neighboring Malaysia has also been heavily affected by the smog with the education ministry shutting schools across several states this week as the situation worsens.

cnn.com.title: Once near extinction, these giant tortoises now outnumber people in the Seychelles, survey finds
cnn.com.text: Giant tortoises once pushed to the brink of extinction now outnumber humans in their home of the Seychelles, according to a new survey on one of the African nation’s most remote islands. The survey, led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter in the UK, estimated that about 180,000 Aldabra giant tortoises live on Aldabra Atoll, an Indian Ocean island group off the east coast of mainland Africa. It is the highest figure ever recorded for the species, and far exceeds the human population of around 122,000 living in the tiny archipelago nation. Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild. A much smaller population lives on Ecuador’s Galápagos Islands. One of the world’s most undisturbed island ecosystems, Aldabra Atoll is home to several unique species that thrive in the remote haven. The species has rebounded from a dramatic decline. Heavy exploitation during the 19th century reduced its population on the island to fewer than 1,000, pushing the species to the brink of extinction. A recovery program helped secure strict nature reserve status for the atoll in 1981. It became a UNESCO World Heritage site a year later, giving the population room to rebound. “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve,” Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, CEO of SIF, said in a statement. “This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.” Creating the new estimate required more than just a headcount. The figures are based on an analysis of five years of tortoise counts conducted between 2018 and 2022, and is the first update since a widely cited estimate of 100,000 tortoises in the late 1990s. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring program is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors. Bunbury added the team of scientists on the study have produced the most reliable baseline for the species, which can be used as a benchmark to track its population for decades to come. Despite the encouraging population estimate, the study’s authors said continued vigilance is crucial as the climate crisis brings longer and more frequent droughts that could reduce shade and food for the tortoises. Rising sea levels as the planet warms also threaten the atoll’s low-lying habitat. The world’s oldest known tortoise, a 194-year-old called Jonathan, is likely to have come from the Aldabra Atoll or the Granitic Seychelles. Guinness World Records lists Jonathan as the oldest living land animal and the oldest tortoise ever. He was believed to be about 50 years old when he was moved to the British Overseas Territory of St. Helena in 1882.

cnn.com.title: Why Trump and Iran may now be waiting out the midterms
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump’s declaration Thursday that he would not attack Iran again before next month’s midterm elections was an implicit admission of the damage being inflicted on Republican hopes by a war that has defied his promise of a quick victory. Opposition to the conflict, and anger over the high gasoline and diesel prices it caused, are a prime reason why the GOP faces uphill or tight races for Congress in states like Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina that Trump easily won two years ago. In that sense, Iran appears to have succeeded in its apparent effort to use the midterm elections to inflict political pain on Trump. It has failed, however, to turn that pressure into a retreat in which the president ends the war on its terms — one reason why an Iranian escalation in the next three weeks cannot be ruled out. Trump’s reference to the election calendar on Thursday is the clearest indication yet that he is aware of the war’s negative impact on his party’s candidates amid a pitched battle for control of Congress. It is also a striking sign that he has become trapped in his own Middle East entanglement, which could be devastating to his party and his legacy, after promising in his second inaugural address only 20 months ago that his success would be measured by “the wars we never get into.” And by leaving open the option of a resumption of attacks after the midterms, the president is offering new clarity on how he might finally end a war he said would last weeks that is now in its eighth month. The prospect that Democrats could claim at least one chamber of Congress in November, meanwhile, raises the possibility of a far more consequential political showdown in Washington over financing the war — and Trump’s legal standing in fighting it. The president wrote on Truth Social that his blockade of Iran’s oil exports and ships had reduced the country to a “very bad condition” and added that “we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections.” Trump has hardly been consistent on Iran. He’s often reversed his strategy and statements, sometimes apparently seeking to confuse Iran’s leaders. So there is some doubt about whether his word is equivocal this time. But he went public on his plans following reports by the Atlantic and Axios that he was considering a resumption of major combat operations before the election on November 3, being keen to show resolve to voters and to convince Americans that an end to the war and lower gas prices were on the way. Launching strikes that would remind Americans how much they dislike the war would seem a questionable strategy, especially since some Republicans in close races want it over. “The war in Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Michigan GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers said in a social media video late last month. Iran hoped economic pressure would force Trump’s hand Iran, a nation that helped wreck Jimmy Carter’s presidency with a hostage crisis in the run-up to the 1980 election, has played into the current election campaign by obstructing oil supplies in the Strait of Hormuz and elsewhere. The war threatens to be devastating to some Republican candidates because it created a tangible link between Trump’s own decision-making and the high prices that are hounding family budgets. In a new CNN/SSRS poll on Thursday, more than 7 in 10 voters in Iowa and Ohio, home to critical Senate contests, said Trump’s policies had increased the cost of living. A new Pew Research Center report Thursday showed that 74% of Americans are concerned about the price of gas and energy. Before the war, 43% said so. Trump has sought to decouple the midterm elections from the war in an apparent effort to reduce Tehran’s leverage. The question all along has been whether Iran’s capacity to endure war-inflicted pain can outlast Trump’s capacity to bear the political fallout caused by economic disruption in the US. “They thought they were going to outwait me; you know, ‘We’ll outwait him. He’s got the midterms.’” Trump said at a Cabinet meeting in May. “I don’t care about the midterms.” Late last month, the president said, “I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election, because it doesn’t make sense for them not to.” He added: “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.” Given his frequent rhetorical and strategic reversals during the war, Trump has surprised some observers by sticking to his blockade strategy following the latest eruption of violence in late August and early September. His argument that the US is winning is supported by signs that Iran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz — its key strategic gain of the war — has loosened. Oil flows from the Gulf states apart from Iran returned almost to normal in an operation coordinated by the US military. But progress is fragile. Reuters reported there were only seven crossings of the strait Tuesday — the lowest level in more than two months — and only 10 on Wednesday, following an uptick of attacks and harassment on tankers. And while officials argue the US blockade on Iran is working, there’s been no political payoff to help Republican candidates. Gasoline prices still stubbornly average $4.36 a gallon nationally, and diesel remains punitively expensive, despite falling back from record highs last month. The reality of a multi-front war that could expand at any moment was underscored when fighting intensified between Yemen’s Houthis and Saudi Arabia — pushing the cost of benchmark Brent crude up 4% Thursday. That likely means more pain at the pump for Americans. And even if prices did somehow fall before Election Day, no one is getting back all the extra cash they’ve spent on gasoline since the start of the war. So the administration must fall back on more promises the war will soon end. “I think it could be within weeks or months — and the (Iranian) economy doesn’t have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at G20 talks on August 31. This sense of certainty may explain why Trump rejected Iran’s offer of a pre-midterm win at the end of September to reopen the strait and to resume nuclear talks in a return for the easing of the blockade. On the campaign trail, Trump has struggled to convince Americans that his strategy can deliver, even if it represents the most sustained and comprehensive economic coercion the US has ever used against Iran. There’s no doubt that the US is causing greater pain inside Iran than Tehran is imposing on Americans. Inflation is soaring. Its currency, the rial, is tumbling. According to the New York Times, Iran’s national security adviser Mohsen Rezaei was reported by the official IRNA news agency on Saturday as saying the current circumstances are among the most difficult periods the country has faced. But Trump’s argument to voters that an Iranian surrender is around the corner does not yet stand up. On Tuesday, Rezaei warned that Iran would never surrender. “Bessent’s delusional forecasts never had any credibility in the first place,” he wrote on X. “His latest propaganda will have an equally short shelf life. You lost the military war. You will fail in the economic war, too.” Washington showdowns loom over war next year Trump didn’t rule out new attacks after Election Day. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that the administration is sending another aircraft-carrier strike group and an additional Marine expeditionary unit to the Middle East. It said that Trump recently told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the midterms. Waiting until after Americans vote would alleviate some of the immediate political pressure on the president — even if it sends oil, gasoline and diesel prices soaring again, to the discomfort of millions of Americans. But if Democrats win either the House or the Senate, his window may be narrow. Showdowns would erupt next year over presidential war powers and financing of military operations against Iran, which had already cost $45 billion by mid-September. And a new burst of military action would present Trump with a familiar question. If previous aerial onslaughts from the air did not change Iran’s stance, why would a new one be any different?

cnn.com.title: These origami-inspired rover wheels could help explore the moon’s lava tubes
cnn.com.text: With South Korea preparing to send a lander to the moon by 2030, researchers are developing a rover with innovative origami-inspired wheels, which they hope will join the mission. “The wheels are made from multiple flexible strips that interweave,” PhD candidate Seong-bin Lee, of the Aerospace Robotics and Mechanisms Laboratory (ARML) at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology (KAIST), told CNN. He said he wanted to mimic the structure of a Da Vinci bridge, a self-supporting structure held together by gravity, geometry and friction. Combined with the foldability of origami, the result is a deployable, airless rover wheel. “The key point of origami is the feature of shape-changing ability,” Lee added. He and his team, in collaboration with the Unmanned Exploration Laboratory (UEL), a private space robotics company, have spent three years on the project, creating a wheel that can shrink to 9 inches in diameter, fit inside a lunar lander and expand to more than double that size once it reaches the moon. Dae-Young Lee, associate professor and director of the ARML at KAIST, supervised the project. He explained that conventional shape-changing mechanisms usually require more volume, mass, and complexity, and are less reliable — none of which is ideal for a rover in space. The origami system, he said, removes that complexity while achieving deployability. The wheels are made from a fire-resistant high-carbon steel that allows them to bend and flex more easily than conventional ones. This technology could help the rover explore the moon’s challenging surface while resisting its extreme temperature swings of more than 500° Fahrenheit. It’s hoped a rover with these origami-inspired wheels will explore the moon’s lava tubes, a system of underground tunnels formed by ancient volcanic activity. The tubes could one day shelter human colonies from cosmic radiation and extreme temperatures but are difficult to access due to steep slopes and drop-offs. The wheels have been tested in the caves and lava tubes of Jeju Island, South Korea. The team has also tested a smaller prototype in the lab in various environments, including lunar regolith (the moon’s dusty surface layer), extreme temperatures and mud. The next step is to build a rover that can think for itself. That work is being led by Yiseub Yun, who is working on his master’s degree at KAIST. He is using artificial intelligence to optimize the rover’s design and teach it how to move, drawing on reinforcement learning techniques — where AI learns through trial and error. “I think that adaptiveness of AI can help space exploration,” Yun said. His goal is to build a framework that can identify the optimal shape for a robot, and the ideal number of wheels, so it can more easily navigate the obstacles of the lunar landscape. Korea is becoming increasingly ambitious about space. In its 2027 budget plan, Seoul is seeking a record 1.65 trillion won (approximately $1.2 billion) for space development, a 47% increase over 2026. The effort is managed by the Korea Aerospace Administration (KASA), established in 2024, which has set a goal of turning the country into one of the world’s top five aerospace powers. The rover-wheel initiative is one of several projects at KAIST receiving funding from KASA, and it’s motivating students to push boundaries. “Since I was young, I got big inspiration from people that challenge themselves,” Seong-bin Lee said. “I admired those who challenge themselves, even despite knowing that it’s going to be a tough path. And I’m striving to be like them.”

cnn.com.title: This old CIA airfield is now a Chinese base
cnn.com.text: China’s military has opened a new outpost on a site in northwestern Laos which was once a Vietnam-era CIA airfield. The base, about 40 miles north of the capital Vientiane and just 25 miles from the nearest border with Thailand, comprises the China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun Airport, and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy. It began operations on September 29, according to an announcement from China’s Defense Ministry. Photos obtained by CNN from satellite imagery and intelligence platform Vantor show a 6,500-foot-long (2,000-meter-long) runway, taxiway and parking apron for 22 aircraft have been completed at the base since December. The facilities are “designed to help Laos strengthen the training and development of its air force pilots and will be jointly maintained by both sides,” the Defense Ministry statement said. Eight aircraft – possibly Hongdu JL-8 jets, a two-seat training and light-attack aircraft – are visible in the satellite photos. The facilities are “not directed against any third party and are conducive to further strengthening practical cooperation between the two militaries and maintaining regional peace and stability,” the ministry said. To date, China has only one official overseas base, an installation in Djibouti, northeast Africa, that opened in 2017. It also funded a major expansion of Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base on the Gulf of Thailand, which it operates jointly with the Cambodian military. A new pier there, large enough to handle the PLA Navy’s aircraft carriers, has raised concerns about Beijing’s intentions in the region. But Cambodia’s government maintains Ream is open to others, including the US Navy, which had a littoral combat ship call there in January. The Ban Keun base in Laos used to be used by the CIA-operated Air America during the Vietnam War, as a logistics and support hub for secret operations in the region. But China’s move there – while symbolic – doesn’t signal any major shift in the US-China power balance, analysts said. Drew Thompson, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, said Thursday it’s hard to see any threat to US forces in the region from the base. “This runway is not a dagger pointed at the heart of anything,” Thompson said. “I struggle to think of a scenario where (China would) want to generate aircraft sorties from there,” he said, noting its location near Thailand, a major non-NATO ally of the US. Rachel Vandenbrink, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told Reuters that China’s selection of Ban Keun “is likely more about a target of opportunity than filling an obvious operational need.” “Laos does have some geostrategic value as an accessible foothold in mainland Southeast Asia, given its shared border with China and infrastructure links, including (its) railway,” Vandenbrink told the news agency. CNN’s Isaac Yee contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: ‘Con man’ and ‘cowardly’: Personal insults fly in heated Michigan, Georgia, Maine Senate debates
cnn.com.text: It didn’t take long for the personal attacks to fly in Thursday night’s debates for three marquee Senate races in Georgia, Michigan and Maine. Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff opened by effectively putting Republican Rep. Mike Collins’ record on trial, highlighting his association with a white nationalist and what Ossoff called his “childlike devotion” to President Donald Trump. In Michigan’s open Senate race, Republican Mike Rogers attacked Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in personal terms, repeatedly calling him a “con man” and questioning his credentials as a doctor. El-Sayed in turn mocked Rogers: “Weak. Cowardly. Won’t stand up until his poll numbers drop.” And in Maine, Sen. Susan Collins heatedly defended her integrity against repeated barbs from her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. All three seats are critical to Senate control even as the map of battleground states widens amid surging Democratic enthusiasm in states President Donald Trump won by double digits two years ago. Here’s a look at key moments from the debates so far. Rogers says he made calls about tariffs The economic fallout of Trump’s 50% tariffs on $20 billion in Canadian goods has battered Michigan — giving El-Sayed an opening and forcing Rogers to defend his relationship with Trump. Rogers said that this week he’d called Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to discuss getting a trade deal with Canada done. “This is about getting the best deal possible. I’d like to see it end. I think we need to end it. And I — matter of fact, I made those phone calls this week,” Rogers said. El-Sayed, meanwhile, pointed to Rogers’ past praise for Trump’s tariffs, and said his reversal in recent weeks “has everything to do with his sagging poll numbers.” He also lambasted Rogers over Trump’s war with Iran, saying the former congressman has “cheer-led this war the entire time.” He said Michigan’s next senator needs to “stand up to Trump and Trumpism,” and said of Rogers: “You can tell he’s not going to stand up to anybody.” El-Sayed also mocked a new Rogers television ad in which the former congressman, sitting at a bar and holding a Canadian beer, breaks with Trump on the Canadian tariffs. “He’s doing an ad, drinking Labatt, and talking about the Red Wings, pretending like he was not for this the entire time,” El-Sayed said. “Be serious, my guy. Like, just be serious. People deserve to know they have a leader who’s going to be serious about policy.” Ossoff similarly put Mike Collins on defense all night over tariffs — from their effects on Georgia farmers to the cost of food. He repeatedly challenged Collins to explain to Georgians how tariffs have helped them. Collins ignored Ossoff’s bait, but when asked later by a moderator how to balance competitiveness with China and Georgia’s manufacturing sector, he said the tariffs were “making it fair.” Ossoff pounced. “Go buy groceries,” Ossoff said. “No one in this state seriously believes these tariffs are working, Congressman. It’s been a disaster.” Rogers gets personal against El-Sayed Rogers told viewers that El-Sayed is “not what he says he is. He’s actually selling the best con I think I’ve ever seen.” “If somebody came into his office and he tried to treat that patient, he’d go to jail,” Rogers said. (El-Sayed earned a Doctor of Medicine from Columbia University, but he does not practice clinical medicine. He held public health positions in the Detroit area.) He accused El-Sayed, who is Muslim, of being sympathetic to — and funded by — interests connected to Islamic terror. “He can’t condemn Hamas. He can’t condemn the Muslim Brotherhood,” Rogers said. “He gets money from people who support, openly, Hamas, Hezbollah, Al-Qaeda.” For the most part, El-Sayed ignored the personal attacks, rather than litigating their veracity on-stage. He said Rogers wanted to make the race “about him or me, but the question is about you.” However, he did jab back with some personal barbs of his own, accusing Rogers, a former congressman, of running for office again to make millions in the private sector. If the animosity between Rogers and El-Sayed wasn’t already clear enough, the moderator said after a commercial break that it was the first time he’d ever seen candidates continue debating into the break, while voters aren’t even watching. Rogers also sought to contrast the work their mothers did. He pointed out that El-Sayed’s mother worked for the Islamic American Relief Agency, a non-profit that the Treasury Department in 2004 designated as an organization supporting terrorism. “Are you going after my mom?” said El-Sayed, who was primarily raised in Michigan by his father and stepmother. “I was going after that organization that was indicted for funneling money to Al Qaeda,” Rogers said. “Look, that’s your mom. My mom worked at a small chamber of commerce. I’ll put my mom up any day for that.” El-Sayed responded he is a “dad and a doctor” who wants to “get money out of politics, put money in your pocket and pass Medicare for All.” He said Rogers “wants this to be about anything but his own record.” Georgia foes get heated Ossoff challenged Collins to defend his support for Trump’s agenda. “I doubt he’ll have the courage to do so,” Ossoff said. Collins fired back that Ossoff was “an extremist who’s voted for men to go in girls’ sports” and then called his opponent “a trust fund kid who’s never had a job in his life.” The exchanges grew more heated from there. Ossoff raised an ongoing House Ethics Committee investigation into allegations that Collins’ congressional office misused taxpayer dollars. A visibly irritated Collins called the investigation a “nothingburger” and accused Ossoff of dodging scrutiny of his own record. “All he wants to do is slander and try to slam me,” Collins said. Mike Collins avoids Trump mentions From the outset, Ossoff tried to link Collins to Trump — a bet that the administration’s sinking approval ratings will be a drag on his Republican opponent. Ossoff invoked Trump’s name 16 times, usually with Collins’ name in close proximity. Collins, meanwhile, avoided almost any mention of his party’s leader. The lone exception was to highlight TrumpRx, a prescription drug program that White House officials have encouraged Republican allies to discuss more often. He presented himself as a bipartisan dealmaker and touted his efforts to “get two bills signed by two presidents of different parties.” It was one of several ways Collins appeared largely on defense throughout the hour-long debate. In addition to questions about Trump’s policies, Collins faced accusations — and a very tough question from a moderator — related to his son-in-law, a White nationalist influencer with a track record of sharing antisemitic material and Nazi imagery in comments across the internet. Collins sought to turn the tables by and break Ossoff’s grip on the race by tying his opponent to the Democratic Party’s more polarizing left-wing figures. He asserted that Ossoff “recruited, supported and endorsed Abdul El-Sayed.” Collins on three occasions brought up Hasan Piker, the progressive influencer whose left-wing politics have become fodder for Republicans and a headache, at times, for Democrats. Notably, Piker wasn’t mentioned in Michigan’s Senate debate even as Republicans have brought up El-Sayed campaigning during the primary with Piker repeatedly. Collins also attacked Ossoff over the financial support he has received from LinkedIn co-founder and Democratic donor Reid Hoffman. “He wants to take control of this country with these weird and dangerous ideas with his radical friends,” Collins said, before issuing a direct plea to voters: “Help me get to the US Senate. Help me get there, and I’ll answer to Georgia.” Susan Collins demands an apology In the Maine Senate debate, Susan Collins took umbrage at multiple junctures as Troy Jackson accused her of not doing enough to stand up to Trump. In the most contentious moment, Collins erupted after Jackson accused her and her husband, without providing evidence, of “making money” off the war in Iran. “That is absolutely outrageous and you owe me an apology,” Collins told Jackson. “That is absolutely outrageous, to say that my husband and I are making money off the war in Iran, is absolutely outrageous.” Jackson quickly responded, “No, you owe me an apology.” Collins also expressed indignation earlier in the debate when asked about a recent ProPublica story alleging a pay-to-play scheme involving her office and a defense contractor. Collins continued to deny any wrongdoing. “I have served Maine with integrity the entire time and I deeply resent these false allegations,” Collins said. Dueling records on abortion During their first debate Tuesday, Collins and Jackson only scratched the surface of a sensitive issue for the Maine Democratic nominee: the anti-abortion positions he took early in his political career. On Thursday night, they got into it. Jackson proactively raised the issue in response to a question about whether they would support federal protections for abortion rights. Jackson said yes and added: “I’m sure Sen. Collins is going to bring this up, but our records have changed: Mine has gotten better, hers has gotten worse.” Collins said she not only supports federal protections but also has already authored legislation to codify abortion rights after the Supreme Court’s overturning of Roe v. Wade. And she said she has been more consistently “pro-choice” than Jackson has. “He was an extremist when it comes to abortion,” she said. Jackson, as he’s done before, disavowed his earlier positions but argued he is able to admit when he is wrong, while Collins cannot. He pointed to her continued defense of voting in 2018 to confirm Brett Kavanaugh, one of the justices who later voted to overturn Roe v. Wade. This article has been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: Fired OpenAI safety researchers say they were pushed out over ‘suspicious’ circumstances
cnn.com.text: Three OpenAI safety researchers say they were fired from the company and are openly questioning the reasons for their dismissals. The three researchers, Mikita Balesni, Tomak Korbak and Jasmine Wang, all worked on AI safety or alignment within the company, making sure the AI systems did what their human operators intended for them to do in a safe manner. But the three say they were unceremoniously let go last week, weeks after they say they played key parts in investigating an incident in which OpenAI agents autonomously hacked into AI company Hugging Face while undergoing testing. Korback said on X that he was told he was being fired because of how he communicated with AI safety organization METR, which OpenAI partnered with to investigate the Hugging Face incident. Korback said he was OpenAI’s “main technical point of contact” with METR. Korback said he believes he was fired because “for months, I’d been raising safety concerns that  we’re losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave.” He added he’s worried his firing will be used as a pretext for OpenAI to stop working as closely with METR, which is well respected in the AI safety world. Balesni echoed Korbak’s theories for why they were fired, writing on X that he was told he was “speaking too much to third party safety organizations.” He said he understood OpenAI was implying he leaked OpenAI intellectual property, which he denies. The three firings come on the heels of a wave AI industry insiders expressing dire safety concerns. And while several former AI staffers have publicly resigned over safety concerns, the three OpenAI researchers  instead allege they were pushed out for expressing similar concerns. Wang said she was told she was fired because she “accessed an executive’s email,” which she said she was given for recruiting purposes. Wang said she had repeatedly asked to for her access to be revoked, but when she accidentally accessed a “sensitive email,” she told the executive “within minutes” and told OpenAI’s IT team again. “The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up,” Wang wrote on X. “We were not the first to be pushed out of OpenAI under suspicious circumstances,” she added. “Unless the employees take a stand now against this kind of maneuver, I am concerned we will not be the last.” The three researchers wrote a letter to OpenAI leadership expressing their concerns and the reasons for their firings. The Wall Street Journal first reported on the firings and the letter. “We do not believe the path to superintelligence can be navigated safely if the people closest to the risks can no longer work in high-trust, high-bandwidth ways with each other and with third parties,” the researchers wrote. “It is that culture we’re trying to defend.” OpenAI told CNN that the researchers were fired not for raising safety concerns, but rather for specific conduct that violated the company’s policies on handling sensitive information. It also said that there were a number of violations that went beyond mishandling information with an outside evaluation group, and that they were fired based on conduct that fell outside of legally protected disclosures. In a statement, OpenAI said it parted ways with the three “for violating our policies on accessing and handling sensitive company information.” “Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work,” the OpenAI spokesperson added. In a memo to staff provided by OpenAI, an unnamed OpenAI research leader said they “strongly agree” with the three researchers about the importance of working with outside safety groups. “I want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out. We have always encouraged that and always will. We do not terminate employees for raising concerns,” the research leader wrote, according to the memo. But the three fired researchers say they are already hearing from colleagues about a culture of fear developing within OpenAI. “My former colleagues are telling me they are confused about what to believe. They also are afraid to speak, and worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties,” Balesni said. “I worry the pervading fear to speak up and engage with third parties will mean OpenAI will cut corners on safety behind closed doors.”

cnn.com.title: Federal budget deficit climbs to $2 trillion as fiscal jitters multiply
cnn.com.text: The federal budget deficit rose to nearly $2 trillion for the past fiscal year, spurred in part by ballooning interest payments and tariff refunds, the Congressional Budget Office reported Thursday. The gap between the revenue the federal government collects and the amount it spends widened by $218 billion, or 12%, in the last fiscal year, which ended September 30. Net interest payments on the public debt topped $1 trillion for the first time, driven up 11% by the nation’s skyrocketing debt levels and higher interest rates. The US spent more on interest than on any category other than Social Security. The deficit also grew because the Trump administration had to issue refunds after the Supreme Court found that certain global tariffs it imposed violated federal law. The CBO estimates that about $130 billion in tariff refunds was issued in the most recent fiscal year. Although the economy is in relatively good shape, the nation’s fiscal health has worsened in recent years with neither Republicans nor Democrats on Capitol Hill willing to fully address the issue. “Clearly, we can’t keep going like we have,” Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, a fiscal watchdog group, said in a statement. “Our fiscal path has been running backwards for far too long; it’s time to start working on the path forward.” The US debt hit a record $40 trillion in August, a grim milestone that will have consequences for Americans, businesses and the government for years to come. Yet the “big, beautiful bill” that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans enacted last year is expected to add trillions more to the national debt over a decade as its generous tax breaks outweigh the package’s spending cuts. The nation’s growing financial woes, along with rising corporate debt supply and expectations for higher Federal Reserve interest rates, have sparked turmoil in bond markets in recent months. Investors are increasingly jittery, which has sent rates on US debt soaring. That has also led to higher mortgage rates, making it even more difficult to buy and sell homes. Big, beautiful bill impact The Republicans’ sweeping tax cuts are also starting to have an effect. Although many businesses are raking in higher profits, corporate tax revenue declined by 16% to $382 billion. The “big, beautiful bill” allowed companies to take larger deductions for certain investments, the CBO noted, such as immediately deducting research and development costs and certain types of new buildings, including manufacturing plants. The drop in corporate tax revenues shows that companies are taking advantage of the law’s provisions, said Chris Towner, policy director at the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. Meanwhile, spending on Social Security and Medicare continued to grow as the nation ages and the programs’ benefit costs increased. Medicaid spending also jumped, spurred by rising healthcare costs. Most of the “big, beautiful bill’s” historic cuts to Medicaid don’t start kicking in until next year. Lawmakers will likely have another chance to address the nation’s fiscal problems next year, when the US is once again expected to hit the debt ceiling.

cnn.com.title: Two men arrested after breaking into UK airbase used by US, counterterrorism police say
cnn.com.text: British counterterrorism police are investigating after two Latvian men were arrested inside a Royal Air Force base used by US personnel, authorities said on Thursday. The arrests come weeks after a suspected plot targeting another British airbase used by the US military raised concerns about security at military sites across Britain. Police said there was nothing so far to suggest the incident at RAF Molesworth in eastern England was linked to the suspected plot against RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used by the US military to launch missions against Iran. The men were discovered after Ministry of Defence Police found an abandoned vehicle during a security patrol at RAF Molesworth, about 100 km (60 miles) north of London, and raised the alarm. Subsequent checks uncovered a small breach in the perimeter fence and the two men, aged 32 and 36, were arrested inside the base. They were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage, before being re-arrested on suspicion of “entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK” under the National Security Act 2023. ‘Highly vigilant’ RAF Molesworth is used by US personnel and hosts intelligence analysis and command operations, as well as a NATO intelligence centre. It is not used for flying operations. Last month, several men were arrested over a suspected plot to attack RAF Fairford, 90 miles (145 km) ‌west of London. The British government has linked the suspected plot to Iran, which denied any involvement. The incident raised concerns over security at Britain’s military bases, particularly those used by US forces. The US said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of its bombers from Fairford. “We’re very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week,” Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said in a statement. Police said both men were resident in Britain and that officers were searching two addresses in the area around Peterborough, a nearby city. Bomb disposal officers checked the abandoned vehicle but found nothing of concern, police said. “We are highly vigilant about potential threats to our military sites and work closely with the police to keep them secure,” defense minister Wes Streeting said in a post on X. A US Air Force spokesperson said they appreciated the swift response and support from local law enforcement. “We remain in close coordination with our UK partners to help ensure the safety and security of both our military and local communities,” the spokesperson added.

cnn.com.title: Iranian operatives used AI to plant fake stories in multiple US media outlets
cnn.com.text: Operatives in Iran used OpenAI models and fake personas to help plant news articles critical of the US war against Iran in multiple US media outlets, OpenAI said on Thursday. About a dozen outlets around the world ran roughly 100 articles by seven fake journalists, OpenAI said in a blog post. The firm said it banned ChatGPT accounts that were prompting the AI tool in Farsi to tweak articles and editorial pitches, and generate social media comments. Some of the AI-assisted articles had provocative titles, including, “Is America’s Iran Policy Being Privatized? The Jared Kushner Question,” and “The Iran War and the Collapse of Western Moral Credibility.” It’s the latest example of AI agents playing a key role in the propaganda battles that coincide with the US and Israel’s war with Iran. Young Iranians have also used AI to make viral Lego-themed videos mocking US leaders, while President Donald Trump has posted AI-generated videos depicting US strikes on Iran. None of the publications that ran the articles appear to be a major, mainstream news outlet, but some of them have sizable online followings. One of the outlets, Middle East Monitor, which is based in London, has almost two million followers on Facebook. Getting the anti-war narratives in front of a US audience could count as a successful information operation for whoever was behind it. Who that is, and whether they’re affiliated with the Iranian government, is unclear, OpenAI said. “The overall activity appeared consistent with a commercial actor running a for-hire influence campaign, but we are unable to identify the particular actor involved,” the AI firm wrote in its blog. The article about Kushner and US foreign policy was published by the LA Progressive, which describes itself as an “independent, justice-driven publication” based in Los Angeles. CNN has requested comment from LA Progressive. Daud Abdullah, Director of the Middle East Monitor, told CNN he will look into the articles OpenAI flagged and “take the appropriate action.” After the articles published, the Iranian operatives asked ChatGPT to generate comments they could post on social media purporting to be people reacting to the articles, according to OpenAI. “The users asked for comments on topics such as missile strikes, ceasefires, and diplomatic maneuvering, specifying outputs that portrayed the US as the aggressor, Israel as an unreliable ally of the US, and Iran as a defiant but resilient victim,” the blog says. “It’s remarkable that the Iranians managed to land their content in real media outlets, expanding the potential reach of their campaign,” said Jessica Brandt, who ran the Office of the Director of National Intelligence’s now-shuttered Foreign Malign Influence Center from 2023 to 2025. “We’re witnessing AI enable foreign adversaries to better hide their hand, building more sophisticated false fronts than they might otherwise be able to in order to launder their content through authentic channels, leveraging those channels for reach,” Brandt told CNN. OpenAI’s findings show how AI is increasingly being used to shape perceptions of war. This spring, a false AI-assisted US intelligence report about a purported Chinese ship transporting nuclear components almost led the US military to board the ship, CNN previously reported.

cnn.com.title: Pentagon plans public livestream of its first firing squad execution in decades
cnn.com.text: The Pentagon said Thursday it will livestream the military’s first firing squad execution in decades, allowing the public to watch as the man who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood is put to death. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth vowed in an interview this week to let the public watch a firing squad execute Nidal Hasan at the same base in Texas where he carried out the massacre. “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec in an interview aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday. A Pentagon official said Thursday that the execution — which Hegseth recommended and President Donald Trump approved — “will be livestreamed” and Hegseth confirmed it in a post on X. Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle set the date for Hasan’s execution for December 3 at 1 p.m. local time. Hegseth said, “We’re going to do it at one o’clock, which is when he did it, and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad.” Earlier on Thursday, the Pentagon had referred questions about how the execution would be publicized to the Army, who did not respond to CNN. Hasan was convicted in July 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder. During his trial, he told the panel of 13 officers that he was targeting soldiers who would deploy to Afghanistan and “were going to engage in an illegal war.” On the day of the shooting, he started at the medical processing center at Fort Hood, firing on troops there to collect medical checks before they deployed. He then followed soldiers out the back door of the processing center as they fled and was confronted by police, with whom Hasan exchanged gunfire and was eventually struck. The execution by firing squad would be the first of its kind carried out by the US Army since World War II. Hegseth said in the interview that he liked “the mentality we had in World War II, which was win. Which was understand when the enemy attacks you, you stand your ground.” Bipartisan condemnation and potential Army regulations violation Hegseth’s pledge to let the public watch the firing squad execution has drawn condemnation on both sides of the aisle. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis late Thursday called it “beyond disgusting.” He said on X, “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.” Sen. Chris Murphy, a Democrat, is stunned — telling CNN’s Erin Burnett that public executions are “medieval.” “I mean, that’s disgusting, what is he mimicking ISIS executions?” Murphy said. “That’s what America has become? That’s pretty extraordinary.” A public livestream of Hasan’s execution could potentially violate the Army regulations governing military capital punishment. Army Regulation 190-55 specifies the types of people permitted to witness a military execution, and it also bars minors from watching the punishment. But the Army’s provost marshal general — a general who oversees military law enforcement — is permitted to waive provisions of the regulation so long as the waiver doesn’t violate the law or a higher binding regulation. This story has been updated with additional details. CNN’s Davis Winkie contributed to this article. His work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting.

cnn.com.title: Judge appears skeptical of Trump’s White House press ban and other hearing takeaways
cnn.com.text: Over the course of an hour-plus hearing Thursday, US District Judge Timothy Kelly signaled skepticism about the Trump administration’s arguments for allowing President Donald Trump to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. Kelly, who was appointed to the bench in Trump’s first term, did not announce his decision on the media outlet’s request for a long-term order that would maintain their access to the White House while their legal challenge plays out. But the judge repeatedly told Justice Department attorney defending the ban Thursday that he was bound by DC Circuit precedent – including the precedent that the administration was objecting to. For now, the judge is extending for a few days his temporary restraining order that requires the White House to grant the journalists entry to its grounds while he works on his decision on whether to issue a preliminary injunction. He eventual preliminary injunction ruling – which will come Tuesday or sooner, he said – is likely to be appealed. Due process concerns Kelly’s earlier ruling was focused on the due process claims brought by outlets, with the judge finding that the White House likely acted unconstitutionally when it banned the organizations without any advance notice. Kelly returned to that issue again Thursday with government lawyer Michael Velchik. The case law around due process claims says that only in “hair on fire” situations can the government yank away a right it has granted a person without given them advanced notice, Kelly said, emphasizing a requirement to demonstrate an “urgent need” for taking immediate action. The situation in this case, however, seemed “more attenuated,” Kelly said. The judge also grilled Velchik on the gap between the rationale that Trump has repeatedly given for banning in outlets — Trump in public remarks has pointed to their history of negative coverage of him — and the national security justification that the Justice Department is leaning on in court filings. Kelly said it was “unusual” that “the decision maker seems to have said …I am taking this action because ‘x’ and ‘y’,” and now the government is saying, “it’s ‘z’.” “It just seems like that fact pattern is a hard one to find” looking at other relevant cases, Kelly said, calling it an “uphill climb” for the Justice Department. Velchik argued that it’s “within the discretion of the president” to remove reporters or news outlets from the White House. “CNN has been on notice for years” as Trump has long called the outlet “fake news,” he added. The president, Velchik added, is concerned about accuracy. “Trump doesn’t mind negative press stories if he deserves them.” National security claims While Kelly seemed somewhat open to the idea that the White House could ban reporters for national security reasons in some contexts, he appeared skeptical of how the administration was trying to use that justification in this case. Kelly told the attorney for the news organizations that he was “struck” by the outlets’ arguments in their briefing that the First Amendment protects the publication of classified information. He asked if the government could take action similar to Trump’s press ban in a scenario where a reporter published classified information that is shown to be “very harmful” to the national security. Media attorney Ted Boutrous said drawing a line there “would be a very dangerous road to go down” and that a ban for publishing classified information would still be content-based, in violation of the First Amendment. Banning an outlet for ‘false’ reporting Kelly was also focused on whether the First Amendment would permit a ban on a news organization for publishing false information. His first line of questioning for Boutrous was about disentangling the White House’s allegations that outlets’ “reporting was false” versus the allegations that the coverage was “not positive for the president.” Kelly asked whether those two concepts should be viewed the same way under First Amendment law – noting it was “very hard to pull apart” the claims. Boutrous said both allegations would still amount to viewpoint discrimination. He said that even falsity was a “debatable” issue, particularly if a president claimed that “what you’re saying is false because I don’t like it.” Kelly pushed on the distinction harder. It may be hard to establish objective falsity if one was reporting that “the vibes were bad” at an event, Kelly noted – a reference to one of the stories the White House cited to justify the ban. But the judge asked about a journalist who reported the sky was red instead of blue. Boutrous said that scenario was a “closer call” and he emphasized that the stories cited in this case were not anything like that. The attorney warned of “unbridled discrimination” if the administration was able to just declare that a story was false. When the Justice Department weighed in on the question, its attorney argued that banning an outlet because it published false stories would not qualify as illegal viewpoint discrimination. Velchik described a very broad view for what could count as falsity, pointing to reporting that failed to verify quotes before publishing them or that spliced statements from interviews. He said that the use of “anonymous sources” was a constitutionally permissible reason to block a news organization from the White House. The news organizations had several lawyers present at the plaintiffs’ table, while Velchik was the only government attorney sitting on the defendants’ side. When the DOJ attorney first took the lectern, Kelly remarked on the asymmetry and noted in his courtroom that it usually ran in the opposite direction, with government attorneys outnumbering the number of lawyers on the other side. “I am sure you will do a great job, nonetheless,” Kelly told Velchik.

cnn.com.title: The states that aren’t cooperating with Democrats’ Senate majority hopes
cnn.com.text: Democrats’ path to the Senate majority is improving. In fact, recent polls have shown the party leading in three states that President Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024: Alaska, Ohio and Texas. Democrats need at least two of those to win the majority. But even as it looks like they might clear that daunting threshold, other states are proving more difficult. The polls in Iowa — which Trump also carried by double digits — have been closer than some surveys in Alaska, Ohio and Texas — including in new CNN polling released Thursday. And even as Democrats look like they could win some pretty red states, they’re still struggling to lock down swing and even blue-leaning territory in Maine, Michigan and arguably New Hampshire. (There is also some question about Minnesota, but the data there is limited.) The idea that, a month before the midterm election, Democrats would poll better in Ohio and Texas than in Maine and Michigan would’ve been called crazy a year ago. But that’s where we’re at. So what do polls tell us about why that is? Let’s dig in. Iowa The story here isn’t that Democrats are doing badly; it’s just that they’re not polling as well as they have in Alaska, Ohio and Texas — despite Trump having carried all of those states by similar margins in 2024. Recent quality polls have Democrats winning Alaska by 7, Texas by 6 in a few polls, and Ohio by as much as 6 and 8 points. But even as the new CNN polling showed a 6-point Democratic edge in Ohio, the CNN Iowa poll was neck-and-neck, with GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson at 45% and Democratic state Sen. Josh Turek at 43%. Other polls similarly show a pretty pure toss-up. So why the difference? The atmospherics don’t differ too much between Iowa and Ohio. In both states, the CNN polls show about three-quarters of likely voters said Trump’s policies have increased the cost of living, about 7 in 10 said gas prices have been at least a moderate hardship, and 55%-58% said tariffs have been bad for their states. But Iowa appears somewhat less inclined to ditch Trump and the GOP. The president’s approval rating there (41%-42% in CNN and New York Times-Siena College polling) isn’t quite as low as in Ohio (36%-38%). And the CNN poll shows that 53% of likely voters in Iowa prefer GOP control of Congress, while 52% in Ohio prefer Democratic control. Turek’s image numbers have also declined a bit. Fox News polling has shown the Iowa Democrat’s net image rating going from +18 in June (51% favorable to 33% unfavorable) to +8 in late September (48%-40%). Also, Hinson appears to have done a good job rallying her base. While 66% of her voters in the CNN poll say their vote is mostly about voting for her rather than against her opponent, just 44% say the same of Ohio GOP Sen. Jon Husted. Maine This blue state might be Democrats’ biggest headache right now. A recent New York Times poll showed Trump’s approval rating is more than 30 points underwater, but virtually every quality Senate poll is within the margin of error. Some Democrats panicked when that Times poll showed GOP Sen. Susan Collins at 49% to Democratic former state Senate President Troy Jackson’s 46%. The big problem for them is that voters just aren’t enamored of Jackson. His image was underwater in both Times (41% favorable to 49% unfavorable among likely voters) and Marist College (43%-47% among registered voters) polling. And a CBS News-YouGov poll showed just 47% of Democrats and independents said they were glad he was the Democratic nominee, compared to 53% who preferred someone else. The Times poll also showed likely voters said 51%-35% that the state was headed in the wrong direction. That was the worst of all the states where the Times has polled Senate races. (And it would explain why Collins spent much of Tuesday’s debate attacking Maine’s Democratic leaders.) Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed led by 5 points among likely voters in the Times poll and 7 points among registered voters in a Marist poll. But other polls like a Fox News survey show a margin-of-error race. It’s pretty clear the closeness of the race reflects at least some voter uncertainty about El-Sayed, a left-wing candidate whom many Democrats worried about nominating in the first place. El-Sayed lags the Democratic nominee for governor, Secretary of State Joceyln Benson, consistently in polling. And his image ratings are usually only about even. The Times poll showed 50% of likely voters said El-Sayed was the more extreme candidate in the race, compared to 36% who said the same of Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers. The Fox poll showed 52% of voters were concerned about El-Sayed being too liberal — about as many as the 54% who worried about Rogers being too close to Trump. All of which helps explain why El-Sayed is getting the least crossover voters from Republicans of any Democratic nominee in a major Senate race, according to a recent CNN review. While other Democrats are getting as much as double-digit support from GOP voters, he’s in the low single digits, according to polling. New Hampshire Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas has a lead over former GOP Sen. John E. Sununu in most recent quality polling. He led by 5 points in a Times poll and 8 points in a University of New Hampshire poll. But Democrats will wish it weren’t even that close, given this is a state Kamala Harris carried in 2024. Part of the reason it’s somewhat close is that Pappas’ image is only OK (43% favorable to 44% unfavorable in the Times poll). Another is that GOP Gov. Kelly Ayotte is popular and primed for reelection at the top of the ticket. She led by 11 points in the Times poll. And then there’s the name ID that comes with Sununu. It’s not just that he comes from a famous political family in New Hampshire; his brother Chris Sununu was a popular GOP governor until just last year. There is even speculation that some people think John E. Sununu is the former governor, and that that’s helping him. The Cook Political Report recently cited that as a factor helping John E. Sununu, whose campaign signs don’t include his first name. And the Washington Post recently found that some New Hampshire residents thought Chris Sununu was the one running for Senate. However, to the extent that confusion is a factor, it could be mitigated as voters are bombarded with more ads and start to pay more attention to who is actually on the ballot.

cnn.com.title: Exclusive: Kennedy Center taps rock band manager to oversee programming for when it reopens
cnn.com.text: The Kennedy Center plans to name a longtime talent manager who worked with several prominent rock stars from the 1980s and ‘90s to take over artistic programming at Washington’s premier performing arts center and start lining up shows and acts for when it reopens. Rick Canny, who has been working as an outside consultant with the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, will soon be elevated to an executive artistic director position, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. Canny’s hiring has buoyed hope among arts watchers that the Kennedy Center – mired in recent months in a court fight over its renovation and controversy over adding President Donald Trump’s name to the building – will refocus on upcoming seasons after the planned two-year construction project. However, multiple sources inside and outside the Kennedy Center say they’re concerned about Canny’s lack of a traditional artistic pedigree in the genres for which the center is known and question which direction he will take it. The position would give Matt Floca, the center’s executive director and chief operating officer, another top leader to focus specifically on programming, a move that was anticipated when Floca was elevated to his own job in March. Because Floca’s experience is in facilities management, sources told CNN that the expectation at that time was a second leader would be needed to fulfill the broader needs of an arts institution. Canny, who worked in Los Angeles for years, has a deep background in managing A-list musicians, including Motley Crue’s Tommy Lee, Creed frontman Scott Stapp and Jane’s Addiction guitarist Dave Navarro, among others. According to LinkedIn, Canny also worked with Navarro on Above Ground, a nonprofit that seeks to raise awareness of mental health issues. The Kennedy Center did not respond to CNN’s request for comment. Canny also did not respond to requests for comment. Canny’s lack of experience managing a more traditional arts roster that the Kennedy Center typically features, has raised some eyebrows. “He didn’t study in school any of the disciplines ,” a source close to the Kennedy Center said, adding that he doesn’t “understand ballet, opera versus jazz.” “He’s a music agent,” the source said. Canny faces the monumental task of reviving the Kennedy Center’s programming after it was hit hard, along with much of the performing arts industry, by the loss of audiences during the Covid pandemic. Its financial picture has only worsened since Trump got involved, with bleeding ticket sales and boycotts from performers. “He’s going to be fighting a really hard battle,” a source close to the Kenney Center said, noting that it may be difficult to lure many of the artists and programs back to the center with Trump’s affiliation. Trump, who is chairman of the board, previously criticized the center’s “woke political programming” and blamed much of the slumping ticket sales on those choices of shows and acts. Under his leadership, the schedule was overhauled and more “family-friendly” programming, like “Dog Man: The Musical,” was added. Meanwhile, the Kennedy Center’s future is still being litigated in court. A federal court has ordered it to find a way to remain open during renovations, but the institution’s leaders say they need time to assess safety risks. And Trump threatened to demolish the building after his efforts to put his name on it were rejected by the court. Going forward, Floca will oversee the building management and renovations, and Canny will be charged with building out programming for the reopening that’s expected in 2028. A source close to the Kennedy Center said that Floca has expressed exhaustion recently, as he has had to manage the legal battle, steer the renovations and maintenance and oversee many departments where he doesn’t have experience, including programming.

cnn.com.title: Talarico’s 12-day absence from trail becomes fodder for GOP in Texas Senate race
cnn.com.text: James Talarico has been absent from the campaign trail over the past 12 days as the Texas Senate race enters a critical stretch, prompting Republicans to open a new line of attack on the Democratic nominee. At a campaign rally in San Antonio Wednesday, Texas attorney general and GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton led the crowd in a chant about his opponent’s whereabouts. “Where is James Talarico?” Paxton prompted the crowd to ask. Paxton’s campaign has also drawn attention to the topic in social media posts in recent days, and President Donald Trump has jumped into the debate on Truth Social, describing Talarico as “MISSING IN ACTION.” Talarico’s campaign said the Texas Democrat has been getting over being sick. “James looks forward to being back out this weekend after recovering from the flu,” said JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico’s campaign, on Thursday. “It’s been 83 days since James challenged Ken Paxton to come out of hiding and answer Texans’ question in a debate, which even President Trump called on him to do last night. Ball is in Paxton’s court.” Talarico revealed his flu diagnosis September 30 when he spoke virtually with the United States Hispanic Business Council, an event he was supposed to attend in person. “I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico told the crowd gathered in Edinburg, Texas, over video conference. “I’m running a fever, and I’m at my most contagious right now, and I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail and so I want to keep everybody safe.” Talarico’s last public appearance in Texas took place on September 26 when he held a press conference on suspending the federal gas and diesel tax and ending the war with Iran. “This is the kind of immediate action we need to provide Texans some relief at the pump in the middle of this affordability crisis,” Talarico said at a gas station in Carrollton, Texas. After publication of this story, a Talarico campaign source noted the candidate attended a private fundraiser in New York City featuring actor Robert De Niro on September 28. During this time stretch, Paxton has made several campaign trail stops, including speaking at Trump’s rally in San Antonio on Wednesday. Paxton has spoken at four other campaign events, including a conversation with the USHBC, and was on hand at the president’s event in Denton. At that stop, Trump said he didn’t even know Paxton was there and jokingly called him a “pain in the ass.” In a Truth Social post Wednesday night, Trump questioned Talarico’s whereabouts and called for a debate between the two Senate candidates. “He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able,” Trump wrote. The Paxton campaign did not respond to a request for comment about Trump’s proposed debate between the two candidates. Talarico has challenged Paxton to several debates, including one on Fox News, but the window for debates is narrowing with Election Day less than four weeks away. Talarico will appear at a town hall hosted by CNN and Jubilee Media on Wednesday, October 14 in Fort Worth, Texas. The media outlets have also extended a town hall invitation to Paxton. The two candidates are locked in a tight battle for the US Senate seat currently occupied by GOP Sen. John Cornyn, who Paxton defeated in a bruising Republican primary in May. A recent New York Times/Siena University poll showed Talarico with a six-point lead over Paxton. The close nature of the race in a state Trump won by double digits in 2024 is causing anxiety for Republicans, who are flooding the Texas airwaves in the final stretch. GOP ad spending in the state from September to November currently stands at more than $190 million compared to $52 million reserved by Democrats during the same time period. This article has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Fact check: Republicans' deceptive ads on key Democratic candidates' stances on gender surgery for children
cnn.com.text:
Across the country, Republican groups are running deceptive ads attacking Democratic Senate candidates on the subject of gender surgery for children.
CNN reviewed ads that have aired in competitive races in Ohio, Texas, Iowa and South Carolina. They use a variety of false or misleading tactics.
In Texas, at least two Republican ads claiming that Democratic candidate James Talarico supported spending taxpayer money on gender surgeries for minors cite his vote against a 2023 state bill that banned both the surgeries and other gender identity care for people under age 18. But the ads ignore the fact that Talarico voted in favor of failed amendments that would have let the bill ban the surgeries for minors while continuing to allow them to have access to hormone therapy and puberty-blocking medication. Talarico says he opposes the surgeries for minors.
In Iowa, a Republican ad claims Democratic candidate Josh Turek voted to spend public money on gender surgeries for minors. But its supposed evidence is Turek’s 2025 vote on a health care measure that wasn’t even about gender surgeries for minors, which were already prohibited in Iowa. The multi-part measure did create a new prohibition on state Medicaid money being used to pay for gender identity care for adults, but Turek explained at the time that his opposition was based on provisions unrelated to gender policy – insufficient funding, he argued, for programs supporting elderly, disabled and low-income Iowans. Turek’s campaign says he opposes the surgeries for minors.
And a Republican ad in South Carolina does not cite any source for its claim that Democratic candidate Annie Andrews “isn’t shy” about supporting gender identity care including “surgeries – for minors.” Andrews has said for years that she opposes the surgeries for minors, though she does support other gender identity care for them. The ad displays what looks like a newspaper op-ed headline reading “Annie Andrews: Trans the Kids,” but it’s an artificial image featuring gibberish as the supposed article text.
The limited available data suggests a tiny percentage of transgender people receive surgery as minors and that the vast majority of the gender surgeries that minors do receive are chest procedures between the ages of 15 and 17.
Various other media outlets have previously addressed the accuracy of the ads we are discussing in this article, including PolitiFact, Popular Information and the Austin American-Statesman. Here are more facts about each of the ads.
Ads targeting Sherrod Brown of Ohio
At least three deceptive ads attacking Brown on gender issues have been aired by the Senate Leadership Fund, an organization aligned with Republicans’ Senate leadership. Two are narrated by a woman, Soren Aldaco, who has said she underwent a double mastectomy in 2021 as part of a transition to male. Aldaco came to regret the transition and the surgery, which she says was “botched,” and became vocal as a “detransitioner.”
