Asked for comment, Senate Leadership Fund spokesperson Chris Gustafson noted that Aldaco has said she was prescribed hormones as a 17-year-old minor at an appointment she was taken to by her stepmother rather than the mother who had legal authority over her. Aldaco defended her comments on similar grounds, highlighting that she was a minor when she began identifying as transgender and receiving gender identity care.
But Aldaco didn’t say in the ads themselves that she was 19 or “a college kid” at the time of the surgery. Rather, shortly after mentioning the surgery, she said in each ad that she was “a kid.” Coupled with the ads’ focus on gender surgery “for minors,” Aldaco’s comments in the ads leave the clear and false impression that her surgery, not just her previous treatment, occurred when she was a minor.
Brown released a response ad this week in which a narrator says, as an image of Aldaco is shown on screen, “Seen these ads? They’re a complete lie. Records show not only is this woman actually from Texas, she didn’t have any surgery as a minor.”
The Senate Leadership Fund has run another ad on the same topic. It begins: “Abused and exploited by an extremist agenda. Forcing childhood sex-change surgery. But Sherrod Brown stands with these extremists.” This ad cites no sources, and there is no evidence Brown has supported “forcing” surgery on children or anyone else, as PolitiFact noted last week.
Both of the ads that feature Aldaco cite the same Columbus television news segment from 2023 for the claim that Brown supports gender surgeries for children. We couldn’t track down the full clip, but the Brown quote the Senate Leadership Fund has previously cited as evidence is this: “A child’s health care decisions are between them, their parents, their families, their doctors, not politicians. I will never agree with anybody that wants to bring politics into the family situation with health care, period.”
Brown made that comment in response to a question from WSYX ABC 6 journalist Darrel Rowland. Upon request this week, Rowland, who is now retired, provided a transcript of the exchange. He had asked Brown a question about his relationship with then-Ohio senator JD Vance, noting at one point that Vance had just introduced a bill “dealing with what he called genital mutilation, making gender-affirming care illegal” (for minors). Brown’s reply is open to interpretation, but it didn’t specifically mention surgeries, and the question he was addressing also invoked “gender-affirming care” more broadly.
Brown released a response ad in September that pointed out it’s illegal in Ohio to provide gender surgeries on minors – that’s been the case since 2024 – and dismissed this Republican attack as a distraction from important issues like high prices. It did not specify a Brown position on the surgeries in general.
“In Ohio, this is already settled law. Sherrod is focused on taking on the rigged system and improving the lives of Ohioans,” campaign spokesperson Lauren Chou said in an email this week, going on to criticize Brown’s Republican opponent, Sen. Jon Husted.
Ads targeting James Talarico of Texas
Wealthy Trump ally Elon Musk’s America PAC has run numerous midterm ads blasting Democrats on gender issues. One of them claims Talarico voted “for taxpayer-funded sex changes on kids.” An ad from Texas PAC, a group connected to the Senate Leadership Fund, similarly says, “Talarico supported using taxpayer dollars for sex-change surgeries on young children.”
Both ads make clear they are basing the claim on the fact that Talarico voted against a Texas state bill in 2023 that banned not only gender surgeries for minors but also other forms of gender identity care for minors, like hormone therapy and puberty blockers; state Attorney General Ken Paxton, Talarico’s opponent and the state’s chief lawyer, has asserted that the prohibition also covers mental health care that facilitates a minor’s transition. But neither ad mentions that Talarico had voted for unsuccessful amendments that would have limited the bill to the surgery ban.
Asked for comment, Talarico’s campaign said he opposes gender surgeries for minors. The campaign pointed to a September interview with Fox News in which he explained his 2023 votes.
Talarico called the 2023 bill “overly broad” and correctly said that “if you go back and check, I voted for a major amendment to limit the bill to banning surgeries for minors.” He added, “As a lawmaker, my job is to try to sift through everything the bill does. And sometimes there’s stuff in it that’s really harmful, and I have no choice but to oppose the bill as a whole. It’s why I try to use amendments, to narrow the focus of the bill so that it does exactly what we intend it to do.”
Asked for comment, Gustafson of the Senate Leadership Fund reiterated that Talarico voted against the 2023 bill. His email acknowledged that the bill also banned hormone therapy and puberty blockers for minors, but it did not address Talarico’s support for an attempt to limit the bill to a surgery ban. A spokesperson for Musk’s group did not reply to a request for comment.
An ad targeting Josh Turek of Iowa
An inaccurate Iowa ad from Musk’s group claims that Turek, a state representative now running for Senate against Rep. Ashley Hinson, “voted to spend our tax dollars on sex-change surgeries for children.” It cites Turek’s vote on a broad 2025 item in the state House.
That measure did multiple things, including provide money for health care and veterans’ services. It also included a ban on state Medicaid funds being used to reimburse various kinds of gender identity care for people of any age. Specifically, it said the money “shall not be used for reimbursement for sex reassignment surgery or associated procedures, including hormone therapy or other medical interventions intended to alter primary or secondary sex characteristics related to an individual’s gender dysphoria diagnosis.”
Even if Turek had voted against the broad measure because he opposed this specific provision, that wouldn’t mean he voted in favor of spending tax money on gender surgeries “for children” as the ad claims. That’s because Iowa had already banned gender surgeries, hormone therapy and puberty blockers for minors in 2023 (in a vote for which Turek was absent).
And according to the speech Turek gave before the vote on the measure in 2025, his vote wasn’t even focused on the gender-related provision. Rather, he spoke of how he thought the measure was inadequate in dealing with a “fundamentally unfair and unjust” long wait list for home and community-based services for disabled people, a big shortage of care workers “that really affects the most vulnerable in our state, the disabled and the elderly,” and a loss of funding for a food assistance initiative, among other issues unrelated to gender policy.
Turek’s campaign told PolitiFact earlier this year that he opposes gender surgeries for children, and a campaign spokesperson said in an email this week: “Josh opposes taxpayer-funded sex changes, and anyone who says otherwise is lying.” The spokesperson for Musk’s group did not reply to a request for comment.
An ad targeting Annie Andrews of South Carolina
Andrews, a pediatrician, said during her unsuccessful 2022 run for a House seat that she had “never” supported gender surgeries on minors and that the hospital where she had worked for more than a decade did not perform these procedures. She wrote on social media in 2024: “You would be hard pressed to find a South Carolinian who is MORE on the record on this issue than me. No. I don’t support gender affirming surgeries on minors. Because there isn’t evidence to support it.”
But an ad this year from Security is Strength PAC, which backs her Republican Senate opponent Sen. Darline Graham, features a narrator claiming “Annie Andrews isn’t shy about her support for medical interventions like puberty blockers, hormones, and surgeries – for minors.”
Andrews is on record supporting “gender-affirming care” for minors in general, including the use of puberty blockers and hormones, on the grounds that it has “been shown to reduce the incidence and frequency of suicide and suicidal ideation in trans youth.” She said last year that such treatments are given to “a subset” of children identifying as a different gender and employed “after many, many, many meetings with pediatricians, endocrinologists, mental health providers.”
But the ad provides no basis at all for the claim she supports minors getting gender surgeries in particular, which she has repeatedly opposed. Instead, the ad displays a fake newspaper featuring an imaginary “Annie Andrews: Trans the Kids” headline above article text that is clearly gibberish if you look closely enough.
Asked for comment, Security is Strength noted Andrews’ public opposition to two pieces of state legislation. One was a 2021 state proposal to forbid gender surgeries, hormone therapy and puberty blockers. The other was a 2024 state law that both eliminated all these things for minors and required public schools to immediately notify a parent if a child requests different pronouns or tells an employee their gender doesn’t match their sex.
None of that proves the ad’s claim that Andrews supports gender surgeries for minors. Opposing legislation that broadly eliminates gender identity care for minors does not mean someone supports surgeries in particular.
Andrews released a reply ad this week in which she says Graham is “lying” about her and that “I don’t support and haven’t ever performed gender surgery for minors.”
CNN’s David Wright contributed to this article.

cnn.com.title: Trump says he will not attack Iran before the midterm election
cnn.com.text: President Donald Trump announced Thursday that he has no plans to strike Iran before the midterm election. “We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump declared on Truth Social, adding that the administration is “having productive discussions” with Tehran and that his main goal is to ensure the country does not obtain a nuclear weapon. The president’s comments come after multiple media reports detailed the administration planning for potential new strikes before the elections — just 26 days away. Trump emphasized that he plans to keep up economic pressure on Iran, saying the blockade of Iranian ports “will remain in full force and effect.” The administration has favored economic punishment over military strikes for months, though it’s seemingly done little to motivate Iranian officials to negotiate. The Treasury Department announced additional sanctions against Iran on Thursday, impacting 17 vessels that officials alleged were part of a “shadow fleet” that Iran has used to ship its oil around the world. The department concluded that they had circumvented existing US sanctions to transport millions of barrels of oil and other petrochemical products to countries across south and east Asia. “Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds,” the department said in its statement announcing the new sanctions. Trump has suggested in campaign trail remarks over the last several weeks that he is considering new military action on Iran, telling supporters he has a decision in front of him on how to proceed. While other administration officials have claimed the war is essentially over, Trump said this week the US still has unfinished business. “They’re a mess. But we still have to finish it off,” he said during remarks at a new shipyard in Maryland on Tuesday. The US president has appeared reluctant to resume the war in earnest before the midterms, however, mindful of the political downsides that could come with renewing an already unpopular conflict. Officials also know that flareups between the US and Iran have caused spikes in oil prices, aggravating cost-of-living concerns that have dragged down Trump’s Republican allies. Still, the president had not entirely ruled out resuming military strikes before the midterms until his post on social media Thursday, according to officials familiar with the matter. They said American military planners have been preparing options for a resumption of hostilities, including targeting Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear targets. Trump and top national security officials have held extensive discussions about the next steps in Iran as they work to find a way to get more ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz. Top administration officials traveled to Camp David last Friday for a discussion on Iran, including longer-term planning on the war, officials said. Trump’s claim of “productive discussions” with Iran came after the president rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz last month. Since then, the US has sent a counterproposal that Tehran says it is considering. An Iranian news agency reported Thursday that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said officials planned to respond “within the next few days.” This story has been updated with additional reporting and developments.

cnn.com.title: Vance signals discomfort after report alleges Kimberly Guilfoyle tried to exchange access for funds
cnn.com.text: Vice President JD Vance said Thursday he took issue with anyone seeking financial gain in exchange for access to Trump administration officials after a report claimed Kimberly Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece, sought funds and offered access to top administration officials ahead of her confirmation. “Obviously I don’t love that,” Vance said when a reporter asked whether he had any reaction to a scenario where an American ambassador tried to exchange access for funds. The reporter did not name Guilfoyle specifically. Eric Deters, a Trump donor and former congressional candidate, told CNN’s Jake Tapper on Thursday that Guilfoyle had asked him for $100,000 to pay off an American Express bill. The Wall Street Journal first reported Deters’ allegations. CNN has reached out to Guilfoyle. A lawyer for the ambassador told the Journal that Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the messages. “So right before her Senate confirmation, she says to me, ‘I need $100,000 to pay off my American Express card, or I’m not going to become Greek ambassador,’” Deters said on “The Lead.” “I said, ‘Kimberly, you haven’t done anything that I’ve asked you to do.’” “There was no question it was a quid pro quo,” Deters alleged. “She knew she was nominated. She tried to cover it up. She wanted to paper it by coming up with this idea that it was for past consulting fees.” Vance, who said he was unsure of the specifics of the episode, reserved further comment during a press conference on visa fraud. But the vice president said in general he was uncomfortable with access-for-pay schemes. “Of course I don’t like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official,” he said. “But you know, I assume you’re talking about a specific case, and I can’t say with confidence that the case you’re talking about is actually reflective of the way you’re describing it,” he added. Deters told CNN that he had initially sought Guilfoyle’s help in drawing the attention of the new Trump administration on some personal tax and legal issues he was facing. “I said, ‘Kimberly, if you help me draw attention to this, when the case settles, I’ll give you a million bucks.’ And she said, ‘Fine,’” he recounted. “And she said that she’d start doing all these things for me.” According to the Journal, Guilfoyle reached out to Deters for the $100,000 days ahead of her confirmation hearing, texting him “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today.” Deters didn’t make the payment, the newspaper reported. Guilfoyle had been with Secretary of State Marco Rubio this week as he visited Greece and gave a major policy speech. When asked about the Journal reporting earlier Thursday, Rubio refused to comment. “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said before he boarded his plane to leave the country, with Guilfoyle looking on. Guilfoyle was nominated to the role in Athens by President Donald Trump in December 2024, prior to him taking office. She had been engaged to Donald Trump Jr. and is close to the Trump family. Guilfoyle is a former co-host of Fox News’ “The Five” and was an assistant district attorney at the San Francisco and Los Angeles district attorneys’ offices before beginning her media career. She abruptly left her position on Fox News in July 2018 and later served as the Trump campaign’s finance chair during his 2020 presidential bid. She later became a key witness to the events leading up to the US Capitol attack on January 6, 2021, and met with the House select committee investigating the insurrection in 2022. In addition to her role on Trump’s campaign, Guilfoyle also helped raise money for organizers leading up to the “Stop the Steal” rally on January 6. CNN’s Piper Hudspeth Blackburn contributed to this report. This story has been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: Trump admin bars Microsoft and other tech companies from seeking permanent residency for foreign workers
cnn.com.text: The Trump administration is suspending Microsoft and some other companies from seeking permanent residency for foreign workers hired through the H-1B visa program, accusing them of taking advantage of the process so that they could replace American citizens with cheaper labor from abroad. Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the tech giant is one of a handful of companies to be barred indefinitely from the Labor Department’s PERM program following an investigation spearheaded by the anti-fraud task force that he chairs. That probe determined that Microsoft laid off roughly 6,000 American workers last year, while at the same time employing 6,300 non-citizens that it had brought to the US by obtaining H-1B visas for them. “The H-1B visa is how the people get into the United States in the first place, and then a PERM program is how those employees stay,” Vance said. “There has been no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused the system more than Microsoft.” Vance and other top administration officials alleged that Microsoft had misrepresented its needs in applying for permanent residency for its foreign workers, arguing that the program is meant only for workers with “hyper-specialized” skill sets that can’t be easily found in the US. Instead, they accused the company of using the program primarily to replace skilled American employees with similarly qualified immigrants who it could pay less to do the same job. “The fraud is that they’re making representations when applying for this program that are fundamentally illegitimate and therefore ultimately illegal,” Vance said. In a post on its website, Microsoft officials disputed Vance’s assertions, saying that 80% of the roughly 6,000 H-1B visa applications the company submitted in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees — not to hire new ones. The rest of its applications were for people hired by the company who were already legally in the US. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings,” Microsoft officials wrote. “We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.” The announcement also raised immediate questions about the timing of the administration’s targeting of Microsoft. In a separate ceremony on Thursday, President Donald Trump is due to award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation. The medal is the nation’s highest honor for technological achievement and is awarded to those who make “outstanding contributions to America’s economic, environmental and social well-being,” according to the US Patent and Trademark Office. Vance downplayed the administration’s decision to punish Microsoft over accusations of fraud on the same day that it hailed the company’s achievements. “Our message to Microsoft is not that we want to harm your company, it’s that we want your company to thrive, but we want it to thrive by employing and empowering your fellow Americans,” he said. “So we’re going to continue to support Microsoft and have a great relationship with Microsoft, but we’re also going to deny them the ability to apply for these permanent residencies until they show that they are going to get serious about putting American workers first.” The Labor Department is also indefinitely suspending software firm Adobe and several IT outsourcing firms from the PERM program, meaning that any new or pending requests for permanent residency for their workers will not be considered. Vance did not lay out any specific steps for the companies to regain access to the process, saying only that it wanted Microsoft and others to “change their behavior, improve their behavior and actually get better.” The move marks the Trump administration’s latest attempt to show it’s cracking down on instances of government “fraud” ahead of the midterm elections, framing the issue as critical to ensuring Americans have fair access to job opportunities and federal benefits. Trump officials on Thursday also announced that they planned to separately investigate several universities over allegations of that they had abused the J-1 visa program, which allows them to bring in foreign nationals as students, researchers or teachers. Under that program, Vance said, officials believe that schools regularly employ workers from abroad as a way to undercut the salaries that they would otherwise need to pay to Americans in those positions. The universities under scrutiny are Harvard; Yale; Stanford; Brown; the University of Pittsburgh; the University of California, Davis; California Institute of Technology; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; and Arizona State University. This story was updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Anthropic’s announcement of a ‘Claude-led’ CRISPR-like discovery is sparking controversy. Here’s why
cnn.com.text: AI executives are betting big on biology. They say their large language models that have already dramatically changed the fields of coding and software development and mathematics can upend biological research in the same way. But one company’s attempt to do so has already set off a wave of skepticism and controversy. Anthropic, the AI and research giant behind Claude, last month said its biology research lab had used AI agents to discover an unusual pattern of DNA in the genetic code of viruses, specifically a “novel enzyme system.” The signature is similar to the microbial system harnessed in gene-editing tools such as CRISPR Cas-9, which is used to modify the DNA of living organisms. The technology is commonplace in labs around the world and won the Nobel Prize in chemistry for its inventors in 2020. Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, said on social media the finding offered great scientific potential. “Today we announced the Claude-led discovery of a molecular machine that we suspect could represent a new gene editing mechanism,” he wrote on X. Anthropic said the discovery had been made “with only high-level direction from our scientists” and shares of companies developing gene-editing technology fell shortly after the announcement. However, some experts not involved in the work said the finding was early and incremental, and far from a genuine breakthrough. “These are very interesting preliminary results, but at this point they don’t demonstrate gene editing or provide a mechanistic picture of exactly what’s happening,” said Aaron Engelhart, an associate professor at the University of Minnesota’s Department of Genetics, Cell Biology, and Development. The Anthropic researchers have not determined what the newfound viral sequences actually do and thus whether they represent a mechanism that has practical applications similar to those used in CRISPR tools, according to a document detailing the research. The research also has not been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal. Scientists, including Engelhart, said Anthropic’s finding definitely warrants further investigation, and a news release from the company quoted Feng Zhang — a professor at MIT and the Broad Institute in Cambridge, Massachusetts and a pioneer of CRISPR genome editing for sickle cell disease treatment among other advances — who called the work “genuinely intriguing.” But just days after Anthropic’s announcement, Mario Rodríguez Mestre, who said he used Claude extensively for his recently completed doctoral research at the University of Copenhagen, claimed his unpublished research describes the same viral signatures. “It is essentially the same finding. This is not simply a case of two groups studying related protein families or similar biological systems,” Mestre told CNN via email. Defining originality Mestre’s claims echo those made by mathematicians after OpenAI, which built ChatGPT, announced it had solved a longstanding and high-profile math problem. They also raise questions about how Claude’s find unfolded. The biologists working at the Anthropic lab said they gave Claude a prompt to search a massive database of DNA sequences for “interesting new examples” of reverse transcriptase, or RT, an enzyme that copies RNA into DNA and thus plays a role in the spread of genetic information in an organism. The company said 950 AI agents, which can independently plan and execute tasks, spent 21 hours searching the data, picking out 3,500 RTs. It narrowed the pool down to the 20 most compelling. For an experienced scientist, this type of analysis can take weeks to months, according to a statement from Anthropic. Then, “one of the agents spotted something remarkable: a repeating pattern of DNA sequences that occurs next to the gene for an odd-looking RT,” the company noted in the statement. “After a thorough analysis it was convinced that it had found a new biological system, and filed a report for human review.” Anthropic said scientists at its biology lab then analyzed and tested the finding, which they described as a “previously uncharacterized” biological system in bacteriophages, a type of virus that attacks bacteria, with a similar structure to CRISPR, which is naturally found in bacteria. Mestre, however, said he had shared unpublished research on his private Claude account, including drafts of his dissertation, analyses and material describing these systems. “I am not claiming that Anthropic deliberately took our work. I cannot demonstrate that,” he told CNN via email. “Either information related to our work somehow reached the model and it was trained on it. The second possibility, which I currently think is more plausible, is that there was considerably more prior scientific knowledge and human direction behind the search than the phrase ‘autonomous discovery’ suggests,” Mestre added, referring to language used in the release. Anthropic did not respond to an emailed request to comment. It’s not unusual in the scientific process for different research groups to converge on the same result, but Mestre’s allegation is serious, and many scientists may think twice in the future about inputting their unpublished results into these tools, said Ilya Finkelstein, a professor in molecular biosciences at University of Texas at Austin. New territory Still, Anthropic’s announcement does suggest that AI is beginning to work with more autonomy in science, said Gustavo Sudre, a professor of genomic neuroimaging and artificial intelligence at King’s College London. “It received a broad direction and then had to use its own judgement about what was interesting in the data. That is a real shift from the usual ‘analyze this dataset for me,’” he said in an email. AI excels at the “needle in a haystack search,” rather than the “imaginative breakthrough,” Finkelstein added. AI tools would help explore domains where students would get too tired or bored with finding an interesting pattern worth further investigation, he noted. “They can pursue a very large number of unproductive paths rapidly,” Finkelstein told CNN. “They are really good at grunt work when orchestrated by experts in the field.” Finkelstein also noted that the Anthropic paper’s lead author is Dr. Peter Yoon, who used to work in the lab of Jennifer Doudna, who is one of CRISPR Cas-9’s architects and shares the 2020 Nobel Prize with Emmanuelle Charpentier. So, Anthropic’s AI agents were guided by people at the top of their fields, he said. “Four of six authors are senior molecular biologists and domain experts. Give that group a heap of compute and frontier models (without safeguards, I’m guessing), and I’m sure we’ll be seeing more interesting bioinformatic discoveries,” Finkelstein wrote in a blog post on his lab’s website. However, other researchers say talk of autonomous AI-driven discovery is hype that gets ahead of the actual science, and models aren’t yet able to generate meaningful results on their own — despite the claims to the contrary. Letting a model comb through data at a scale no human can match does move a field forward, but it doesn’t necessarily herald a big advance, Sudre said. “From experience I can tell you that the gap between ‘interesting pattern’ and ‘useful knowledge’ is where most of the work lives,” he noted. Anthropic launched Claude Science, its tool designed for research, earlier this year. Its rivals have all recently unveiled similar tools. OpenAI has GPT-Rosalind, Microsoft has Quine and Google DeepMind has Co-Scientist. They operate like large language models but also harness specific scientific datasets such as DNA sequences. However, models are only as reliable as the data they are trained on. For example, the strength of Google DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which won the 2024 Nobel Prize in chemistry for decoding protein structures, comes from training the AI system on a narrow, specialized data source collected over decades. AI developers are under intense public scrutiny amid growing concern over rogue AI agents and whether AI companies can adequately police them. Biological discoveries can offer company executives an opportunity to craft a more positive narrative that counterbalances some of the doomsaying surrounding their products. But moving toward significant and tangible findings in the field likely requires integrating the AI models into hands-on lab work through robotics. “Biology is not maths and at some point the intelligence has to be expressed in the physical world through a robot that can do the fiddly one-off experimental tasks that a good student would normally do almost instinctively,” said Yuval Elani, an associate professor in biochemical technologies at Imperial College London. “From what I have seen of robotics and automation we aren’t really close. So it will be a while until we can really justify the hype around AI in biology.” Anthropic says it understands there is a limit to what artificial intelligence can do alone and is investing in “model hardware” that will allow AI agents to safely operate physical devices. Sudre at King’s College, whose work integrates genomic, clinical, neural and cognitive data to predict how mental health symptoms will develop in children, is emphatic that the role of humans in science isn’t shrinking. The risk isn’t that scientists will get pushed out of discovery, but that they’ll get lazy and won’t use their judgment to understand whether a result is meaningful, he said. The next step for Anthropic’s scientists is to do the slow work of physical lab experiments to understand the pattern they have identified, and whether the signature might have a practical use in biotechnology. “Sure, in future some of that can go to robots, too,” Sudre said. “But here is the thing, the questions worth asking in science don’t stay hidden in databases waiting to be found. They come from us — from what we care about, what worries us.”

cnn.com.title: Iran-backed Houthis target Saudi airports for third straight day as they warn of long conflict
cnn.com.text: The leader of the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen has warned Saudi Arabia to prepare for a long conflict, as his group intensified its attacks on the kingdom — targeting its airports and military facilities for a third consecutive day. The group said Thursday it had carried out a new wave of attacks targeting two civilian airports — King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Najran Airport near the southern Saudi-Yemen border — and the Royal Saudi Air Force’s King Khalid Air Base. It claimed the attacks involved both cruise and ballistic missiles and had caused damage and disrupted air traffic. Images posted on X and verified by CNN showed smoke rising over Terminal 4 at King Khalid International Airport as well as what appeared to be a damaged Saudi aircraft, while the Associated Press cited a witness as saying several explosions had been heard in Riyadh, including at the airport. While Saudi authorities have not directly commented on whether the airports were attacked, they said Thursday they had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh and that falling debris had damaged a kindergarten and a medical clinic. The US Mission in Saudi Arabia said it was “aware” of attacks targeting the airport in Riyadh and warned American citizens to exercise heightened vigilance, noting previous attacks on civilian airports in the country and cautioning the conflict “has the potential to escalate.” It warned of possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions, and said US government employees now required “special authorization” to use the airport and remained barred from traveling within 20 miles of the Yemen border. The news comes after three people were killed and 36 wounded over the past two days in Houthi attacks on King Khalid International Airport and Abha International Airport, near the Yemen border. Leader’s warning In a televised speech Thursday, Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi vowed to continue attacking Saudi targets and confronting Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. He warned Saudi Arabia against continuing its military campaign in Yemen, saying his group had the military capabilities and resolve to withstand a lengthy conflict. “The Yemeni people today possess all the determination and elements of strength, regardless of how long the war lasts,” al-Houthi said. The Houthis, an Iran-backed armed group that controls much of northern Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa, have been at war with Yemen’s internationally recognized government and a Saudi-led coalition since 2015. The conflict intensified in July after the collapse of the US-Iran ceasefire, with the Houthis expanding missile and drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities, airports and shipping routes. Saudi Arabia has responded with airstrikes and support for Yemeni government forces. In recent weeks, the Houthis have threatened to broaden the scope of their attacks within Saudi Arabia. In a statement Thursday, they warned employees, engineers and workers at Saudi oil facilities to avoid locations that could become targets of future attacks. The group also renewed previous warnings to airlines, airport operators, travelers and workers at Saudi airports and facilities. “The more the Saudi enemy persists in its aggression and blockade, the greater its losses become,” al-Houthi said. ‘Dawn of Yemen’ The latest escalation comes as Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces continue Operation “Dawn of Yemen,” a major offensive aimed at reversing recent Houthi gains in Yemen. In recent weeks, fighting has intensified along Yemen’s western coast and around the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital shipping route connecting the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Yemeni government forces have claimed to have recaptured several positions near Bab al-Mandeb, Mocha and Dhubab, although the Houthis dispute those claims. On Thursday, Yemen’s internationally recognized government said its forces had carried out 1,729 precision strikes against Houthi targets during the offensive, claiming to have killed 1,370 fighters and destroyed or disabled 300 vehicles and other military assets. The same day, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of escalating its air campaign, claiming Saudi warplanes had carried out 59 airstrikes and missile attacks across Sanaa and several Yemeni provinces over the previous 24 hours, causing civilian casualties. CNN cannot independently verify either claim. However, the Houthis have dismissed reports of major battlefield losses, accusing regional media outlets of exaggerating advances made by Saudi-backed forces. Earlier this week, Houthi missiles landed near Aden International Airport, the main airport serving Yemen’s internationally recognized government, forcing the diversion of a commercial flight from Cairo, according to Yemeni government officials. The Saudi-led coalition said late Wednesday that it responded to that attack by launching a large-scale operation striking 82 Houthi military targets in Saada, Hodeidah, Al-Jawf and Marib provinces. According to the coalition, the targets included missile depots, command centers, communications facilities and weapons stockpiles.

cnn.com.title: In new ad, South Carolina Democrat responds to anti-transgender attacks echoed by Trump
cnn.com.text: Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee in the increasingly competitive race for Senate in South Carolina, is pushing back in a new TV ad after President Donald Trump disparaged her with an anti-transgender slur. In the 30-second spot, Andrews speaks to the camera, wearing a white lab coat with a stethoscope over her shoulder, and says she has always been committed to protecting children as a pediatrician and mother of three. “So I want you to hear me loud and clear: I don’t support biological men playing women’s sports and I don’t support — and haven’t ever performed — gender surgery for minors,” Andrews says. The commercial comes three days after Trump dubbed the Democrat “Annie ‘Trannie’ Andrews” in a social media post. Trump supports her Republican opponent, Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to the seat this summer after the death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham. While South Carolina is a solidly Republican state, the Senate race has drawn more GOP attention in recent days as they confront a tough midterm environment nationally. The top Republican super PAC, the Senate Leadership Fund, recently decided to invest $5 million in the contest. Even before Trump used the anti-transgender slur against Andrews, Graham and her allies had been aggressively attacking Andrews on issues related to transgender people. One TV ad from a pro-Graham super PAC depicts a transgender person ominously approaching a young girl in a grocery store aisle and saying Andrews “has my vote.” Republicans have pointed out that Andrews voiced opposition in 2022 to South Carolina’s law banning transgender athletes from playing on girls’ and women’s sports teams at public schools. In an X post, she called the law “shameful” and promised to “always support trans youth.” “Annie Andrews is bad medicine for South Carolina,” Graham campaign spokesperson T.W. Arrighi said in a statement responding to the Andrews ad. “She is openly lying about her record.” Andrews is part of a crop of Democratic candidates in the midterms who are pushing back more forcefully against the GOP’s anti-transgender attacks after seeing how they hobbled Vice President Kamala Harris in the last presidential election. Andrews and Graham are set to meet for their first — and potentially only — debate on Sunday.

cnn.com.title: At the center of Russia’s plague scare, residents ‘don’t trust’ officials – but have little other choice
cnn.com.text: When the Siberian town of Shelekhov found itself at the center of global headlines over a plague scare, residents might have hoped to be the best informed. But Russians have long been accustomed to living with unanswered questions and opaque governance. So, while the sudden death of 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, sparked concern around the world, residents of the quiet town 12 miles southwest of Irkutsk told CNN they knew little more than the news – and rumors – spreading fast online. Six days after the news broke – and with no official confirmation that Shipilova died of plague, amid calls from the World Health Organization and the United States for more information – the situation appears to have prompted both resignation and skepticism. One 36-year-old resident who only gave her name as Evgeniya told CNN everything feels “normal, as if nothing had happened.” She said she isn’t panicking, but said a friend who works as a pharmacist told her that people had been stocking up on antibiotics when rumors of plague emerged. Russia’s health and consumer watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said Shipilova died of a pneumonia of “unknown” origin. The agency downplayed suspicions that her illness was related to her work but rushed to isolate her contacts. While Russia has kept a tight lid on information, CNN has spoken with residents of Shelekhov – where Shipilova died in the hospital Friday – and the nearby cities of Irkutsk and Angarsk to gain a window into the events of recent days, and scoured official and unofficial media reports for clues. The locals asked to give only their first names for privacy reasons. Despite the Kremlin repeatedly urging people to rely only on updates from the agency, Evgeniya said most people she knows didn’t trust the public statements. “There is no official information, and we don’t trust it anyway. There are a lot of rumors, but what is actually happening remains unclear,” she added. ‘Everything is fine’ Others voiced greater trust in the official narrative. Ekaterina, 26, told CNN that “things are not bad at all” for her – and that she didn’t see any need for concern as everyone who had been in contact with the lab worker had been isolated. “People are not giving in to panic and are carrying on with their lives as usual,” she said. “It’s the 21st century now, and there is treatment for plague. This is not like coronavirus, which was something unknown to people. The outlook is much better. So, to sum it all up: Everything is fine. We are following safety measures and not giving in to the madness,” Ekaterina added. That said, a pharmacist in Irkutsk, also named Ekaterina, told CNN that on Saturday there had been a run on “masks, antiseptics, and tetracycline antibiotics” where she worked, with people stocking up “just in case.” “People were, of course, afraid of getting infected,” the 27-year-old said. “There is no panic now. It only lasted for one day. We are not seeing it anymore. Everything is just as quiet and calm.” Alina, 38, told CNN the situation is “ordinary” other than seeing increased coverage of the situation across social media platforms, which she dismissed as “panic and has nothing to do with reality.” An unnamed Russian clinician who spoke to independent news outlet Lyudi Baikala (“People of Baikal”), which has led the way on coverage of the case, was unconvinced, though, by the Russian health watchdog’s statement that the lab worker’s illness was “unrelated to her professional activities.” Citing the need for laboratory confirmation to take up to 10 days, he was quoted as saying, “it is impossible to definitively identify the pathogen just one day after the autopsy.” ‘A deadly virus’ Residents cited in Lyudi Baikala described measures authorities took to mitigate the spread of the unknown infection. They said that, on Friday night, three vehicles pulled to an apartment block believed to be where the deceased lab worker lived in Irkutsk. They said personnel wearing gas masks and orange suits emerged from the vehicles carrying several containers and began disinfecting the entrances. “The smell was unbearable and very acrid,” a resident of the building - a woman in her 40s – told the outlet. The team that arrived told residents they had been sent by the health watchdog. “We asked what had happened. (The personnel) told us: a young woman had died of a deadly virus, but they didn’t know anything else. They said, ‘We showed up for work, were told to go and disinfect the place, so we came and did it,’” the woman was quoted as saying. CNN cannot independently verify the account of disinfection at the apartment block. One voice highlighting the human tragedy behind the global headlines was that of the mother of the young lab worker who died. Svetlana Shipilova – who was also in quarantine in an Irkutsk hospital – told local media outlet Glubina that her daughter hasn’t been buried yet. “After all, who would bury her when we’re sitting here in detention? She was such a hard worker. A pure, such a pure soul,” she said. Ordinary Russians often demonstrate resilience in the face of pressure, and exhibit a resignation toward state-directed narratives that is part of a survival mindset, rather than tacit support. Yulia, 25, told CNN that people are “no longer surprised by anything,” adding: “Information is always limited. I think it’s like that in every region.” A resident of Irkutsk who was responding to coverage of the case on Telegram used dark humor to describe how Russians perceive the euphemistic language of official statements. “An explosion is a bang. A recession is negative growth. A crash is a hard landing. A fire is smoke. A retreat is a gesture of goodwill,” he commented. “The plague is pneumonia of unknown origin… Anyone who catches this pneumonia of unknown origin should wrap themselves in a sheet and crawl to the cemetery. But do it slowly, because the main thing is not to create problems for the authorities.”

cnn.com.title: Don’t miss the Draconid meteor shower, a celestial event that won’t take all night
cnn.com.text: The Draconid meteor shower will briefly light up the sky Thursday night — and it won’t even keep onlookers out past midnight. The shower is expected to peak at 9 p.m. ET Thursday, but depending on viewers’ location, meteors will be visible into the wee hours of Friday morning, according to EarthSky. The Draconids are best seen from the Northern Hemisphere, but sky-gazers in the Southern Hemisphere might glimpse a few meteors by looking near the horizon just after darkness falls. Fortunately, a waning crescent moon isn’t expected to be bright enough to obscure the shower, in which 10 meteors can streak across the sky per hour. The Draconid meteors move more slowly than those witnessed during other showers, clocking about one or two seconds of visibility rather than a fraction of a second. Unlike most other meteor showers that peak early morning, the Draconids are best seen just after nightfall and throughout the evening hours because of the location of the shower’s radiant point — where the meteors appear to come from in the night sky. The Draconids could bring a meteor storm The shower gets its name because the meteors look like they arc from the direction of the constellation Draco the Dragon. Eltanin and Rastaban, stars that make up the head of the dragon, are in the far northern sky in October, according to EarthSky. Meteor showers occur as our planet passes through debris trails left behind by comets and asteroids, which eject bits of rock and ice as they orbit the sun. The Draconids are the result of Earth intersecting with a trail from the comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner, and occurs in October each year when the planet nears the comet’s orbit. The Draconids are also referred to as the Giacobinids in honor of that comet’s discoverer, Michel Giacobini, who spotted the celestial object in 1900. While the Draconid meteor shower is considered much smaller when compared with larger ones later this year, sky-gazers favor this celestial event due to the possibility of a meteor storm. Meteor storms can happen when a comet’s debris is concentrated close to the comet, rather than spread out, as Earth passes through the trail, and can depend on how close the comet comes to our planet during its orbit around the sun. Hundreds or thousands of meteors can be visible per hour during a meteor storm. The comet 21P/Giacobini-Zinner completes its orbit of the sun about every seven years, with scientists reporting increased meteor activity in September 2018 when the comet came closest in its orbit to Earth. The comet also neared Earth in March 2025 and remains relatively close this year — which means that for this unpredictable shower, an outburst is always possible, according to EarthSky. The best way to watch the meteor shower is to sit in a reclining lawn chair or lie on your back and look up at the sky with a wide view. No special equipment is needed, but if you want the best viewing conditions, it helps to be as far from artificial light as possible. Upcoming meteor showers There are more meteor showers to look forward to as the end of the year approaches. Here are the peak dates to glimpse these dazzling celestial events, according to the American Meteor Society.

cnn.com.title: Russian strike kills at least 33 in eastern Ukraine in deadliest single attack this year
cnn.com.text: At least 33 people were killed on Thursday when a Russian strike caused two public buses to catch fire in eastern Ukraine, local authorities said, making it the deadliest single attack this year. Another 18 people were injured in the attack in Kramatorsk, a city in the Donetsk region, which prompted authorities there to shut down the public transport system and urge people to move to safer parts of the country. “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” said Vadym Filashkin, the head of the Donetsk regional military administration. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.” The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SES) said the Russian strike caused a fire on two buses and in the surrounding area. Police in Donetsk said Russian drones targeted officers who were helping victims of the strike. Police were still working to identify the victims of the strike, with some bodies having to be pieced together from fragments, they said in a statement. Footage they released of the rescue operation shows bodies strewn across the road. Drones can be seen near the scene of the strike as responders load the injured onto stretchers and into emergency vehicles. One emergency worker can be heard asking an injured woman for her name. The woman responds weakly, “Tanya…legs, legs.” Shots can be heard ringing out and the woman is put into an emergency vehicle. Filashkin said he had ordered the suspension of public transportation in the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk in the wake of the attack and called on civilians to move to safer areas. “I urge everyone who remains in the Donetsk region to evacuate to safer regions of Ukraine,” he said. “Russia is bringing death to Ukrainian soil. It is striking our cities, killing our people, and multiplying its crimes every day,” added Filashkin as he offered his condolences to the families and loved ones of victims. CNN has reached out to Russia’s defense ministry for comment. Ukraine’s team heads to the US The deadly strike comes as Ukrainian negotiators are expected to visit the US for talks on Friday and Saturday. A source familiar with the matter told CNN US envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner would meet with Ukraine’s intelligence chief Rustem Umerov and Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky. Zelensky said in his nightly address on Thursday that the talks would last two days and that Ukraine counted on its European allies to join in. He added Umerov and Budanov would also use the meeting to raise the issue of air defenses – a critical issue for Kyiv. Earlier on ⁠Thursday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the war in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate and that Washington remains committed to finding a peaceful resolution to the conflict. “We’d love to see a negotiated settlement to this war ⁠that is permanent, enduring, and fair. And that’s what we’re committed to continuing to do,” Rubio said during a visit to ⁠Portugal. Reacting to his comments, Kremlin ‌spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia agreed with Rubio that ​the Ukraine conflict was at a stalemate. “Yes, we agree with him,” Russian state news agency RIA Novosti quoted Peskov as saying, adding it was up to diplomats to find ways of moving towards peace. “The art of diplomacy precisely involves finding some way out that would allow ‌moving onto ⁠a peaceful track,” Peskov was quoted as telling journalists in Turkmenistan, according to Reuters on Thursday. The past few months have been exceptionally deadly for Ukrainian civilians. Russia has been launching near daily mass aerial attacks against the country, taking advantage of Ukraine’s critical shortage of interceptors. A mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage. In August, 38 people were killed when a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot near the capital triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted hours in a residential area near Kyiv. Both Kramatorsk and Sloviansk are crucial industrial cities close to the front line. Together with nearby Kostiantynivka and Druzhkivka, they form the core of Ukraine’s remaining “fortress belt” in the Donetsk region. Kramatorsk has long served as a strategic rear point for the Ukrainian units serving along the eastern front – and as a place to which exhausted troops could retreat for a few days of rest before their next mission. But a press officer with Ukraine’s 93rd mechanized brigade told CNN last month that is no longer an option due to frequent shelling. The fortress belt has slowly eroded over the past four and a half years. Its southernmost anchor, Kostyantynivka, has now been effectively lost as a stronghold.

bbc.com.title: As freezing winter approaches, Kyiv residents look for shelter elsewhere
bbc.com.text:
- Published
As Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities intensify and autumn's cooler temperatures hint at another tough winter to come, Ukrainians are wrestling with how to meet the twin challenges ahead: Russian drone and missile strikes and the biting cold.
"It was a very difficult winter last year in Kyiv," says mother of two Mariia Shostak, who is now packing her bags and leaving her small flat.
With prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures and frequent power cuts brought about by Russia's attack on the country's power grid, last winter was one of the hardest so far.
"There were some days and weeks that were unbearable. I started thinking I'm not going through another winter like this."
Mariia is not even waiting for winter. Russia's latest assaults on the capital have forced her hand.
"Everything changed in late August and the beginning of September, when Kyiv started being attacked around the clock," she said.
"Earlier, the drones and missiles were intercepted somewhere on the outskirts. Now it was happening in the centre, right above our heads."
After weeks of escalating Russian attacks, which by the end of September had included petrol stations, power plants and key bridges over the Dnipro river, Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko said the city was facing a "very dramatic situation".
Mariia's children, four-year-old Artur and Kira, who's two, were both born after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Unwilling to subject them to another miserable, dangerous winter, she's taking them abroad. They plan to spend the winter in Hurghada, on Egypt's Red Sea coast. It's cheaper than Europe, Mariia explains, and warmer too.
"I don't feel safe in Ukraine in any way," she says.
Polls show that many Ukrainians are feeling the same way, even if not everyone has yet made such a radical decision.
A September survey by the Gradus research company found that 40% of Ukrainians were considering relocating if living conditions continued to deteriorate; 35% said they would not move elsewhere, while 25% were undecided.
"People are thinking about a combination of stress factors," Evgeniya Blyznyuk, Gradus's founder and CEO, told us. "Not just about electricity and blackouts like last winter. Russians are targeting big logistics centres, which means that the population is worrying about products, about food during the winter."
Russia's recent attacks on Kyiv's bridges, petrol stations and schools have increased the sense of danger and foreboding.
For families with young children, the situation feels especially urgent.
Last winter, Iryna, who asked us not to use her surname, says her three-year-old daughter Polina found it hard to cope.
"Sometimes we didn't have heating for weeks and the temperature inside the apartment was zero or five degrees," she tells us. "So being here with a little child that is sick all the time was not OK."
The family's recent experiences have only compounded Polina's difficulties.
"We had two missile attacks this year," Iryna says.
The first explosion, in early June, blew out several windows in the family's home on the north-western edge of Kyiv. A month later, after some of the damage had been repaired, a second blast, close to the foot of their 10-storey apartment block, propelled a wave of earth into the flat, forcing the family to move into temporary accommodation.
Polina's health has deteriorated. She suffers from extreme anxiety, which has brought on bouts of incontinence, vomiting and uncontrollable shaking.
"Now we have this neurological problem with her so that's the reason we're thinking about leaving," Iryna says. "There are new symptoms after each shelling."
Iryna, whose husband is in the army, has not yet decided where to go. Her work with an international NGO may allow her to work remotely from Poland.
"Our president says that it is better to leave Kyiv because this is target number one," she says.
For other Kyiv residents, the solution lies closer to home: in the vast open spaces of Ukraine's countryside.
Olena Konoplia tells us she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital.
"I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explains.
"Everything that can be a Russian target."
On the day we visited, Olena was busy ferrying supplies to the house and supervising the installation of a new door.
In keeping with Ukrainian tradition, a priest has already been around to bless her new home.
The cottage has gas-powered convection heaters, but in an adjacent barn a stack of firewood will help to keep Olena warm in the event of power cuts. She has already installed high-speed internet, necessary for her work at a Kyiv-based charitable foundation.
At a time when air raid sirens sound constantly in Kyiv and explosions can be heard almost every day, the peace and quiet of the village is what Olena says she needs most.
"After several nights here, when I can sleep, just sleep, without any explosions, without any sirens, I feel better," she says. "I can work, write my articles, I feel good."
Olena's elderly mother will soon be joining her.
"She lives in a pretty dangerous district in Kyiv and it's harmful for her health," she explains.
Of course, not everyone can afford a cottage in the countryside or a months-long trip abroad.
Most Kyiv residents will do what they can to survive another tough winter in the capital, just as they have before.
The authorities are taking steps to prepare. Some of Kyiv's most vulnerable citizens – the elderly and women with young children – are being offered places in converted sanatoriums and rehabilitation centres in the city's forested outskirts.
Meanwhile, a network of around 15 small-scale power plants has been constructed around the city over the past 18 months in an effort to shore up Kyiv's battered power grid.
The plants, constructed in fortified bunkers and protected from drone attack by huge steel cages, are each capable of providing electricity and heat to several hundred of the city's high-rise apartment blocks.
But with energy companies already talking about scheduled power cuts and supermarkets experiencing periodic shortages of some goods, the pressures to leave are growing.
Evgeniya Blyznyuk says she does not expect to see a mass exodus from the capital and says most people have yet to make up their minds, reluctant to jeopardise their jobs or take children out of school.
"They will postpone it until conditions become really unliveable," she says.

bbc.com.title: ICE agent shoots man in New York City
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent shot a man in the Bronx in New York City on Thursday.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the agency, confirmed an ICE officer "discharged his weapon" during "a targeted enforcement operation... to arrest a criminal illegal alien".
In a statement, it added the man was alive and at a local hospital.
New York mayor Zohran Mamdani said it was an "unconscionable and incredibly serious situation".
"Early reports indicate agents surrounded him and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds. We believe the child was physically unharmed," he said.
The BBC has approached DHS for comment about Mamdani's remarks.
Late on Thursday evening, New York Governor Kathy Hochul said she had spoken to President Donald Trump about the shooting and had expressed "outrage on behalf of New Yorkers".
"I also asked that any body camera footage of the shooting be released to the public so we can establish the facts and get to the truth."
Trump has not yet commented publicly on the shooting.
The DHS said the man, who has not been named by officials, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs, and weapons possession".
He was arrested by police officers in New York in December 2023 and released "a few days later", according to the DHS statement.
It also claimed he was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group.
Mamdani, meanwhile, said he would ask Trump to end ICE enforcement actions in the city.
"I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorise our communities," he wrote on X on Thursday evening.
New York, which is a Democratic stronghold, is one of several American cities that bars its police officers from assisting with federal immigration enforcement.
A group of protesters gathered at the scene on Thursday evening, chanting "we want justice" and "ICE off our streets now".
There have been several high-profile shootings involving ICE officers this year, including one which caused the death of Renee Good in Minneapolis in January.

bbc.com.title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.
The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.
The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.
In the Federal Court on Friday, lawyers for White Fox denied any breach of trademark.
While White Fox has not yet lodged a formal defence, its lawyers told Justice Ian Jackman that the firm intends to argue that other prominent Australian brands such as Cotton On, Sportscraft and Glassons sell clothes with "similar decorative stripes".
Lawyers for Adidas told the court that White Fox, in advertising and selling its clothes with four stripes, had the "intention to trade off our reputation".
A three to four-day trial is expected to take place early next year, the court heard.
In its written statement of claim, Adidas says its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.
The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.
White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.
It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.
This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.
The company says White Fox is "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".
Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.
Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.
In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.
A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.
In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.
White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.
In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

bbc.com.title: Firing squad execution to be livestreamed, Pentagon says
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The public will be able to watch the execution of a former US Army major by firing squad, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has said.
A Defense Department official told the BBC the execution of Nidal Hasan, who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, would be livestreamed.
It is believed it would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The decision to livestream it is "unprecedented in the modern era" and "on uncertain legal terrain," said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."
The Pentagon announced earlier this week it would execute Hasan in the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Hegseth said in an interview with conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice that Hasan is "gonna get a firing squad of soldiers. As it should be".
Asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to President Donald Trump, Hegseth said: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."
A Pentagon spokesperson said on Monday that Trump had approved the defence secretary's recommendation. The BBC has asked White House whether Trump supports a livestreamed public execution.
While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two countries carried them out publicly.
Eleven public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025, and another six in Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International.
The execution is scheduled to take place at Fort Hood in Texas on 3 December, the secretary of the US Army said on Tuesday. It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, has admitted fatally shooting 13 unarmed soldiers in a crowded medical building at Fort Hood in 2009.
At court he apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law. It also requires appellate review, where a higher court inspects the decision, and a final judgement on its legality to move forward.
The appellate process for Hasan is not over, Mills said, and he is likely to seek review of his conviction and sentence in federal court, which would likely stay the execution.
As such, Mills said that he would be surprised if the execution happened.
"Seeking to make it livestreamed, a firing squad execution, is little more than attention-seeking by the Trump administration and is unlikely to occur, much less deliver any semblance of justice," he added.
Eugene R Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School, told the BBC it was a "really unfortunate decision".
"To livestream an execution is just so out of the Middle Ages. In a way, we are so past that as a society, at least I thought so until today," he said.
Fidell said if Hasan pursued legal action, the "proceedings would last years" and "far longer than President Trump's term in the White House".
Certain states require some form of public viewing of executions. Many states require journalists to be present, and the person due to be executed can invite people. Others also allow ordinary citizens to volunteer as witnesses.
But "there hasn't ever been a livestreamed execution," says Deborah Denno, a law professor at Fordham University, who has studied US execution methods.
A livestreamed execution would "force a level of transparency that we have probably never seen before in this country", she says.
"More than half of the country wants the death penalty - even though that's on the decline - an argument could be made that 'if you want the death penalty, then we are going to show you how it's conducted in this country'. And people would have to realise exactly what's happening in a way that many people ignore."
Denno says there are important considerations for a livestream such as whether it would be age-restricted and whether it would contravene the policies of the online platform that hosts the viewing.
It is unclear where the livestream will be available. Most major social media platforms have rules that prohibit or restrict livestreaming explicit content.
Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook and Threads, explicitly bans any live stream of capital punishment. TikTok has a similar ban. X, which has loosened content moderation since Elon Musk took over, says content showing a person's death will be removed "if we receive a request from their family or an authorized representative."
Truth Social, the social media platform owned by Trump, does not have a live-stream video feature for users.
The countries with the highest number of executions last year were China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the US, in that order, Amnesty International data shows.
The US government had not executed anyone for 17 years until the final year of Trump's first term as president, when it conducted a flurry of 13 executions. Upon returning to office Trump swiftly overturned predecessor Joe Biden's moratorium on federal executions.
The last military execution in the country took place in 1961, when a US Army private was hanged after being convicted of raping an 11-year-old Austrian girl. The execution was authorised by then-President Dwight D Eisenhower and took place despite the victim's family asking his successor, John F Kennedy, for clemency.
The last military execution by firing squad took place in January 1945, when a young US Army deserter, Eddie Slovik, was shot during the final months of the World War Two.
With additional reporting by Kwasi Gyamfi Asiedu and Kali Hays

bbc.com.title: Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem - so why is Meta's business booming?
bbc.com.text:
Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful.
"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make."
Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists.
It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company.
For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users.
That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case.
And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him.
His reputation is unlikely to be helped by The Social Reckoning, a film by Aaron Sorkin released this week. It's about whistleblower claims that Meta executives were aware of their products harming young people. Succession actor Jeremy Strong plays Zuckerberg as a "full-on villain", according to a review in the Hollywood Reporter, "stoically arguing that even the slightest gesture of responsibility is anathema where money is concerned".
Some speculate that this is Meta's "Big Tobacco" moment, with a consensus forming against the company, and the social media industry as a whole.
But the truth seems to be more complicated. Despite months of bad press, in the real world Meta's products are doing better than ever. Use of its apps continues to rise, and users are already flocking to its new AI assistant.
It raises the question: can anything really clip Meta's wings? Or is it now something of a 'Teflon' company, with scandals simply bouncing off it?
Meta's 'trust deficit'
It's certainly been a year of bad headlines for Meta.
Last summer, Reuters revealed that Meta allowed its chatbots to "engage a child in conversations that are romantic or sensual", and provide false medical information to users.
Meta has revised those policies and said that such responses should never have been allowed.
And this year, bills have been mounting. In March, a jury gave $6m (£4.5m) to a 20-year-old California woman who claimed she suffered mental health harms related to her use of Meta's Instagram and Google's YouTube.
Around the same time, New Mexico became the first state to succeed in a lawsuit against Meta over child safety issues. A jury found the company had failed to warn the public about the dangers its platforms posed to kids. Meta was fined a total of $942m. The judge called Meta a "public nuisance" akin to air pollution.
Meta says it disagrees with the verdicts and is appealing both cases.
In May, Meta was among the social companies that avoided a trial by settling a case brought by a Kentucky school district that claimed their product design had led to a youth mental health crisis. Meta reportedly agreed to pay $9m, the most of any defendant.
And this summer, Meta struck a high-profile $18bn settlement with 48 US states, plus the District of Columbia and three US territories. Meta denied wrongdoing as part of the settlement, and during the five-day trial it maintained that it had worked extensively over the years to make its platforms safer for young users, pouring resources into testing and research. As part of the deal, the firm promised to enact two-hour daily time limits for young users, along with night-time blocks on use, muted notifications during school hours, and other changes.
The company faces other lawsuits too, including one starting later this month in Los Angeles, also related to alleged social media addiction among young users.
Meanwhile, several countries have moved to ban social media for children entirely, starting with Australia last December. Social media companies are broadly disliked, even while their products remain wildly popular. A Reuters/Ipsos survey suggests that 85% of Americans think social media can be addictive for children, and 61% support greater government oversight.
To some, the trust issue feels existential
"Once the public has stopped trusting you, it's kind of a downward spiral," says associate professor Alison Taylor of New York University's Stern School of Business.
"It feels like… the trust deficit is so big, I just don't know that they're going to be able to recover."
'Withstanding the blowback'
But despite those high-profile cases, the company reported that the number of people using some of its apps (like Instagram and WhatsApp) has risen 3% year on year and this year's second quarter revenue was up 28% compared with the same period in 2025.
While it has agreed to temper its pursuit of the teen market (which many brands eagerly cultivate to build their future user base), the company has said that teens accounted for less than 1% of its revenue anyway. Competitors TikTok and Google's YouTube are more popular with young users.
And the company's settlement with the 48 states was widely considered a massive win for Meta, because it prevented some Meta bosses (including Zuckerberg) from having to give testimony, and stopped the release of further internal documents, while allowing the company to avoid admitting wrongdoing. The company's stock price surged 4% immediately following the announcement, and is up more than 25% over the last month.
One view popular among critics is that the company has tested consumer tolerance for bad behaviour and until now, its business has mostly managed to withstand the blowback. In other words, people will continue to use the products even if they don't like the company.
"I think they're in a remarkably good position that I didn't expect them to be in," says Patrick Moorhead, founder and CEO of Moor Insights & Strategy.
Meta's new AI agent
However, Meta's move into AI depends partly on rebuilding public trust.
Last month, the company launched its new AI personal assistant app, Muse. Crucially, Muse is an AI agent, meaning it can carry out tasks in multiple stages and work on something over several hours (in contrast to chatbots like ChatGPT, which tend to do one task at a time).
It's the first AI agent from a major tech firm to become publicly available. A New York Times tech reporter who used the app for two weeks says he was "blown away"; the app called his dental insurer on his behalf, ordered him groceries and tracked his credit card spending in a spreadsheet.
