At a summit in Montreal later this month (29-30 October), the EU and Canada will pledge to launch “an alliance for the future”, with a host of agreements on digital trade and the economy, and plans to intensify ties on raw materials, the Arctic and people-to-people contacts.
The nine-page draft summit text seen by the Guardian does not mention the phrase “associate membership”, reflecting scepticism about the term European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen surprised EU diplomats with last month. Canada’s government also appeared to distance themselves from the term, which has no legal basis in EU treaties.
Semantics aside, the two sides will pledge to deepen ties on a long list of areas to build “a deeper and more integrated relationship”. The text, likely to be closely read by the UK and others, states:
“Our partnership may become a model for other countries seeking friendship in a challenging world.”
According to the draft, the EU and Canada will:
sign an agreement on the joint purchase of 50 waterbombers made by Canada’s DeHavilland to be ready by 2030 to fight wildfires in Canada and the EU.
negotiate Canada’s entry into flagship EU programmes, such as Horizon (research) and Erasmus+ (student exchanges and education) and the Galileo satellite programme.
assess options to export Canadian liquefied natural gas and critical minerals to the EU
deepen cooperation on AI safety and carry out feasibility studies on new subsea infrastructure to connect Europe, Canada and Asia
increase labour mobility to reduce barriers to young people and skilled professionals working on both jurisdictions
Ukraine war stalemate could 'quickly turn ... into a much broader ... regional conflict,' Rubio warns
Meanwhile, let’s bring you comments from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, who was in Lisbon this afternoon and warned that the continuing stalemate between Russia and Ukraine was “very dangerous.”
Speaking alongside the Portuguese foreign minister Paulo Rangel, Rubio warned that any escalation “could quickly turn what is a war between two countries into a much broader and far more dangerous regional conflict.”
Rubio said there have been attempts to reach a negotiated settlement, and “we will keep trying”.
Here are a few more images showing the scale of the demonstration currently gathered at Place de la Bastille in Paris…
Left-wing presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon – whose party, France Unbowed (LFI), has long been supportive of the protests – is set to address the crowds shortly.

theguardian.com.title: Florida judge allows lawsuit against Shah of Iran’s alleged ‘chief torturer’ to move forward
theguardian.com.text:
The alleged “chief torturer” for the deposed Shah of Iran is a step closer to trial for human rights abuses after a Florida federal judge rejected his demand to halt a lawsuit brought by three former political prisoners.
Parviz Sabeti, who was reported last year to have lived in a quiet upscale central Florida community, is accused of being the former head of Savak, the shah’s secret police and intelligence agency. The plaintiffs say they discovered his whereabouts only after a photo of Sabeti at a 2023 protest against the Iranian government was posted on social media by his daughter.
He could now be made to answer as early as next year to civil claims under the Torture Victim Protection Act (TVPA) that he directed and took part in the detention and torture of thousands of the shah’s political opponents in jails in Tehran and elsewhere until the Islamic revolution swept the regime from power in 1979.
Sabeti has denied allegations that that he was personally involved or that Savak tortured detainees, and claimed that he “always opposed torture”.
Tuesday’s sealed order by the district court judge Gregory A Presnell rejected Sabeti’s argument that a statute of limitations on the allegations should be strictly enforced and a summary judgment issued in his favor.
In August 2025, Presnell rejected a motion by Sabeti’s lawyers to dismiss the case outright, ordering the parties to conduct discovery on whether the TVPA claim was time-barred, and said he would listen to arguments about why the deadline should not be extended.
Sabeti’s lawyers dispute that he was difficult to find and sue before 2023, filing dozens of documents which they said proved he had lived openly in Florida under his real name, including property records, media articles, and a photograph of Sabeti with George HW Bush and his son Jeb Bush, a former governor of Florida.
In May, attorneys for the three Iranian plaintiffs filed a response presenting dozens of documents and articles of their own to try to bolster their argument that there were extraordinary circumstances in the case that warranted an extension of time to bring the claim.
They included the Guardian’s September 2025 story that chronicled Sabeti’s departure from Iran and his low-profile new life in Florida, where the lawsuit asserts he “has spent the last four decades out of the public eye, concealing his whereabouts and identity”.
As the Guardian reported last year, Sabeti was identified as a fiercely loyal ally of the shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, in a secret analysis by the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) written in 1978, which was not released until 2018.
According to the complaint, he was “widely recognized as one of the most powerful and feared men in the shah’s regime … with the authority to apprehend, interrogate and prosecute opponents throughout the country”.
The plaintiffs, Iranian men living in California aged 68 to 85, claim they were among thousands of people rounded up as perceived opponents of the shah by Savak, Iran’s notoriously brutal internal security and intelligence agency, and subjected to abuses at Sabeti’s personal direction.
Among their claims made under the TVPA are that their captors used rape, electric shocks, near-drownings and forced nail extraction against political prisoners. They say they were abducted by Savak in Tehran, beaten into giving false confessions and served prison time.
The lawsuit details the alleged use of a torture device nicknamed Apollo, an electric chair named after the early US space program, which featured a metal helmet that amplified victims’ screams into their own ears.
Sabeti has previously insisted he was not involved in the detention, torture or execution of prisoners. A 2023 report on the website of the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran, a dissident group, cited an interview Sabeti gave to the Persian channel Manoto in which he characterized his government employment as clerical work.
Court papers list seven attorneys for Sabeti. None replied to the Guardian’s request for comment by the time of publication.
Claret Vargas, senior staff attorney for the Center for Justice and Accountability, an advocacy group representing the three Iranian plaintiffs, welcomed Presnell’s ruling, which she said allows the case to move forward towards discovery on the TVPA allegations against Sabeti. The court previously dismissed the state law claims.
“I’m very glad that our clients will be able to pursue justice after all these years, and everybody deserves justice for torture regardless of who was in charge, or the regime that tortured them,” she said.
“Perpetrators of torture should not escape accountability simply because the survivors were forced to live with fear for decades.
“We don’t yet know the specific legal basis for the court’s decision, but it’s a really important milestone for our clients to be able to bring forth this case and really address [their allegations].”
Donald Trump’s war in Iran has brought new scrutiny of the resilience of the country’s hardline Islamic regime, and the strength of the opposition to it among a sizable Iranian expat community in the US.
Washington DC-based Reza Pahlavi, the former shah’s son, has positioned himself as a possible new leader if the current regime falls, although questions remain over his level of popular support.
In June, Pahlavi, 65, was forced to distance himself from far-right supporters who flew banners and wore shirts with the Savak emblem at rallies.
Divisions between various opposition groups of Iranians in the US were highlighted by the killing in Canada earlier this year of the Iranian activist Masood Masjoody, a critic of the US-led war and the campaign to install Pahlavi as the country’s next leader.
According to the Associated Press, Masjoody’s sudden disappearance in February was followed by a threatening post on X in Farsi directed at other activists by a since-deleted account named for Savak.

theguardian.com.title: Anne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature 2026
theguardian.com.text:
The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded to the Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson, the Swedish Academy has announced.
The academy cited the author’s “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.
The Nobel prize, regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, is awarded for a lifetime body of work. The winner receives 12m Swedish kronor (£900,000).
Ingrid Carlberg, the permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had told Carson of the award on the phone shortly before the news broke. “She had time to tell me that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind,” Carlberg said. “She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”
Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson is known for work that moves freely between poetry, prose and translation, drawing heavily on the literature and mythology of the ancient Greek world. She has been a professor of classics at various institutions including Princeton, New York University and McGill University in Montreal. She is the 19th woman to win, out of 123 literature laureates.
Carson’s first book, Eros the Bittersweet, was published in 1986 and combined literary criticism with an exploration of desire and the ancient Greek tradition.
Her best-known work is Autobiography of Red, a 1998 novel in verse inspired by the fragments of the ancient Greek poet Stesichorus. It reimagines the myth of Geryon, the red-winged monster killed by Herakles, as the story of a modern teenage boy navigating heartbreak and desire.
In 2001, she became the first woman to win the TS Eliot prize, for her collection The Beauty of the Husband. She has also been awarded Guggenheim and MacArthur fellowships.
The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, congratulated the poet on X after the announcement. “With wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own, Canadian poet Anne Carson has reimagined the classics. She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature,” he said, adding that it was a “proud moment for Canada”.
David Leonard, the executive director of the Writers’ Trust of Canada, said: “Anne is such a brilliant writer. Her work is broad, but also extremely smart.” Calling Carson’s work “intoxicating”, he said her four-decade career had resulted in a peerless collection of poems and essays. “They’re beautiful, they’re smart, they’re true and they are humane. It’s exactly what we need in our writing.”
Carson’s work has attracted praise from fellow writers including Susan Sontag, who once said: “She is one of the few writers writing in English that I would read anything she wrote. If there’s a magazine that has something of hers in it, I buy it automatically.”
Anders Olsson, the chair of the Swedish Academy’s Nobel Committee for Literature, praised Carson for work that had “broken away from lyrical poetry bound to the narrative self and inspired new forms of contemporary literature”. He said: “This method of writing leads to playful and ironic works that move not only between classical and modern poetry but also between different genres and artforms.”
Carson’s books have ranged widely in form. Men in the Off Hours combined verse essays, poems, epitaphs and prose about artists and historical figures, and won the inaugural Griffin poetry prize in 2001. Decreation, another eclectic work, brought together poetry, essays and an opera.
Nox, published in 2010, is particularly characteristic of Carson’s avant-garde approach to literature – the book takes the form of an accordion-fold box containing a reproduction of a notebook Carson made after the death of her brother. Her later works include Red Doc> and Float.
In a Guardian review of Red Doc>, Sarah Crown wrote: “To engage so fluidly, so originally and compellingly, with a story first told more than 3,000 years ago, is astonishing: her ambition is one thing; the fact that it is so completely achieved is, frankly, something else.”
Much of Carson’s work has emerged from her fascination with language itself. The Swedish Academy noted: “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” adding that Carson had identified the etymology of words as “the starting point for all her work”.
Asked why she continually moved between forms, Carson said in an interview: “Boredom, I guess. There is a restlessness. There are a lot of forms to try.”
She has acknowledged the difficulties that come with her experimental style. “[My work] does fall apart a lot,” she said in a 2018 interview. “It gets just too weird for anyone to care about reading, or else it gets diluted into a sort of parody of itself.”
Ira Wells, the president of PEN Canada, said Carson’s win felt “particularly significant at a moment in which Canada and Europe are strengthening cultural ties amidst broader global disruption”. He added: “On an aesthetic level, Carson’s verse vibrates on profound human frequencies, at a moment in which more and more language is formulated by machines.”
Carson has generally kept her personal life out of interviews. However, in an August 2024 article for the London Review of Books, she disclosed that she had been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease.
The Nobel prize in literature has been awarded on 118 previous occasions since 1901. Recent laureates include Annie Ernaux, Bob Dylan, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Louise Glück, Peter Handke and Olga Tokarczuk. Last year’s recipient was the Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai, known for his dystopic and avant-garde writing.
Carson, 76, will formally receive the medal and diploma in a ceremony in Stockholm in December.
- To browse works by Anne Carson, visit guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

theguardian.com.title: Russian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontline
theguardian.com.text:
A Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year.
The regional prosecutor’s office in the Donetsk region said on Thursday the vehicle had been hit at 10am by an aerial bomb. “As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” it said, adding that all local public transport had been suspended.
Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. A second bus had also caught fire, officials said. The strike targeted an area next to a dental clinic on the city’s Yuvileina Street.
Three people had also been killed by shelling in the village of Bilenke, outside Kramatorsk, they added. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Kremlin had deliberately targeted an “ordinary public transport stop”.
Some of those killed could not be identified because of the severity of their injuries, Ukraine’s president added. He said the number of victims could “sadly rise”, as doctors fought to save the lives of those wounded.
He said: “This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace.”
The bombing follows a gruesome Russian strike on Wednesday on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The building collapsed, entombing those inside. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, aged between one and eight.
Visiting the scene with Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, Zelenskyy urged the US to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage so that Ukraine could hit targets inside Russia such as launch sites. So far, Donald Trump and Elon Musk have refused Kyiv’s request.
Miliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict” than this week’s murderous attacks. He said: “Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”
Writing earlier on social media, Zelenskyy called on western allies to take “concrete steps” to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences, amid a round-the-clock Russian onslaught in recent weeks featuring ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
“Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day. Important talks with our partners will take place today and tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk form part of a “fortress belt”. They are the last two big cities in northern Donetsk under full Ukrainian military control. Russia has been trying to capture them for more than a decade, after a brief period in which Russian forces occupied Sloviansk in 2014.
The cities are home to thousands of civilians, as well as Ukrainian soldiers. In recent months, roads have been festooned with nets to protect traffic from marauding enemy drones. These defences offer little protection, however, against aerial bombs.
“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” the Donetsk regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, said on Telegram after Thursday’s strike. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”
He added: “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.
“Russia deliberately flouts every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians.”
There was criticism of the White House’s policy of engaging with Vladimir Putin, whom Donald Trump has invited to December’s G20 summit in Miami, Florida. The Kremlin has yet to say if Russia’s leader will take part.
The former US ambassador to Moscow Michael McFaul said on social media that Russia was guilty of terrorism. “There is no other word for it. Putin is running a terrorist state. That officials from my country call this terrorist a nice guy is deeply embarrassing for me.”
Putin has demanded Ukraine cede the rest of the eastern Donbas region still under its control. Kyiv refuses to hand over its territory, believing Russia will take any concessions and carry on fighting.

propublica.org.title: U.S. Lawmakers Launch Sexual Abuse Probe of Youth Sports Giant AAU
propublica.org.text:
What Happened: Bipartisan leaders from the powerful House Energy and Commerce Committee launched an inquiry on Wednesday into the Amateur Athletic Union, criticizing the sprawling youth sports organization for its handling of child sexual abuse allegations and demanding answers, citing reporting by ProPublica and The Washington Post.
What They Said: “It is unacceptable that AAU is failing to implement standard reforms to protect child athletes, and is misleading the public, parents, and athletes about preventative measures in place within AAU sports,” the letter reads.
The committee chair, Kentucky Republican Brett Guthrie, called ProPublica and The Post’s reporting “deeply disturbing” in a statement on Thursday, saying it “raises serious questions about the organization’s actions over the past decade.”
“Our Committee is seeking information on how the AAU’s policies have potentially fallen short, and what needs to be done in order to protect young athletes,” Guthrie said.”
The members of the committee, which in 2018 investigated systemic failures surrounding sexual abuse by former USA Gymnastics doctor Larry Nassar and others, said in the letter that they were “seeing parallels” between its past investigation and “what is being uncovered within the AAU today.”
The letter is addressed to Jo Mirza, the AAU’s president, and asks detailed questions about the organization’s operations, taking the extra step of demanding a briefing from Mirza to the committee by Oct. 21. Among questions about its safety policies and coach training, the committee asks Mirza to lay out how many sexual abuse allegations the nonprofit receives each year and how many coaches it disciplines, information that has long been shrouded in secrecy. The AAU declined to provide the data to ProPublica and The Post. The AAU does not publish a list of banned coaches like many other youth sports groups do, and ProPublica and The Post found that it has used confidential arbitration clauses to keep lawsuits from child sexual abuse victims from being heard in open court.
The letter is signed by Guthrie, ranking Democrat Frank Pallone Jr. from New Jersey and representatives in charge of oversight and investigations.
Background: ProPublica and The Post found that the AAU, which has some 760,000 athletes and coaches nationwide, is failing on nearly every level to adequately protect young athletes from sexual abuse — breaking pledges it made in the wake of a 2011 sexual abuse scandal involving its CEO and young basketball players.
The investigation found that the AAU has become a haven for coaches suspected of abuse, according to a review of public disciplinary lists and interviews with current and former executives from six national sports governing bodies and other key stakeholders.
The AAU, the investigation found, does not offer child abuse prevention training, though it claims to the public that it does. And ProPublica and The Post found that it has suppressed allegations of sexual misconduct, including against another top executive in 2018.
Why It Matters: The committee is one of the key congressional groups charged with overseeing the federal youth sports safety system. It has the power to push for changes in child safety law — and to force transparency from organizations like the AAU, which has repeatedly failed to deliver on past promises of reform.
In 2018, in the wake of the allegations against Nassar, scrutiny from Congress led to the passage of a law known as the Safe Sport Act. It created the U.S. Center for SafeSport, an oversight group, to investigate allegations of sexual misconduct and gave it the power to suspend or ban coaches for life.
But SafeSport has jurisdiction only over national sports governing bodies, like USA Gymnastics and USA Volleyball, that are overseen by the Olympic and Paralympic Committee — meaning much of the law does not apply to the AAU.
The law does require “all amateur sports organizations” — not just governing bodies — to “offer and provide consistent training to all adult members … regarding prevention and reporting of child abuse.” The Energy and Commerce Committee’s letter cites that provision of the law and demands that the AAU explain how it complies.
Response: In a statement, the AAU said, “As always, we will cooperate fully and respond appropriately to any questions or requests from congressional committees or U.S. government agencies.”
Previously, the AAU told ProPublica and The Post that it is “committed to protecting its athletes through comprehensive protection policies overseen by our Compliance Department,” and said it has an “ongoing commitment to providing a safe, secure, supportive, and trusted environment where athletes can thrive.”

propublica.org.title: Club Med, a Disney Cruise and an Exploding Starship: SpaceX Used Bystander Videos to Track Falling Debris
propublica.org.text:
When SpaceX’s giant Starship rocket exploded over the Caribbean last year, the internet lit up with videos from airline passengers, island tourists and locals showing flaming debris shooting across the sky. Even some airline pilots recorded the fiery aftermath as planes scrambled to move out of its path.
Some of those videos of Starship’s seventh test flight — including ones taken from Disney and Royal Caribbean cruise ships and a Club Med resort — went on to play a role in the company’s efforts to count and track pieces of debris after the explosion, a report obtained by ProPublica says.
The report — obtained by ProPublica from the Federal Aviation Administration through a freedom of information request — shows video captured a fireball, then a shower of sparkling debris in the sky moments after the explosion. It includes maps pinpointing where the images were shot, which helped the company understand how debris tumbled to earth after the blast.
“At 1 minute 42 seconds, the debris cloud is observed transiting behind the cruise ship,” says the report, which SpaceX provided the FAA two weeks after the so-called mishap.
Such reports are required by federal rules in the days after a rocket failure and are supposed to describe what happened and where hazardous debris landed. The information is key for the FAA’s efforts to keep busy air traffic corridors safe at a time of rapid growth in the commercial space industry as companies like SpaceX develop and test rockets that they hope will eventually reach the moon and Mars.
During launches, the FAA preventively closes airspace. It has also been forced to clear areas quickly after test flights of massive spacecraft went wrong.
Starship flights 7 and 8 broke apart last year and scattered debris above airline traffic over the Caribbean. Before Flight 9, the FAA moved to greatly increase the size of the airspace it walled off pre-launch.
The agency defined its no-fly zones, which are closed to airplane traffic during a launch, and its so-called debris response areas, which are closed after a mishap, using information from SpaceX and modeling from Space Force, the branch of the military that deals with the nation’s space interests, to predict where debris might fall.
Nearly doubling those pre-launch no-fly zones “only makes sense if the prior margin was judged inadequate rather than just unlucky,” said Moriba Jah, a professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Texas at Austin.
Earlier this year, the FAA issued a warning that rocket launches could “significantly reduce safety” for airplanes, after ProPublica reported that 21 planes appeared to make sudden turns to exit or avoid an FAA-designated emergency no-fly zone in the minutes after the Flight 7 explosion. Such disruptions are likely to become more frequent. SpaceX is seeking to launch Starship up to 76 times a year from Cape Canaveral, Florida.
The FAA provided ProPublica the reports on Starship flights 7, 8 and 9 — all of which involved mishaps — after we requested them under the Freedom of Information Act. The FAA redacted the vast majority of all three reports, citing, among other things, exemptions in the law that protect confidential business information from disclosure. The blackouts were, in part, a reflection of SpaceX’s objections; FAA allowed the company to challenge the release of information it deemed proprietary.
The FAA refused to release information that would show SpaceX’s estimates of where debris fell during the three rocket failures. It’s unclear what the agency or the company knows about how close any airplanes came to falling debris.
“Withholding the underlying debris estimates makes it impossible for anyone outside SpaceX and FAA to check whether that pattern is improving or repeating,” Jah said. “Given a regulator already revised its own safety margins once, the public has a real interest in seeing the data behind both the old margin and the new one.”
The unredacted part of the report did not show whether the debris from the Flight 7 explosion fell where SpaceX and the FAA expected it to. But the references to Disney and Club Med guests’ video suggest SpaceX did not have a full picture of where the debris landed without them. “I would read it as evidence their own tracking did not carry cleanly through the debris cloud phase, so they used the public to fill the gap,” Jah said.
SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment. The company has said that it learns from its mistakes and that each test improves Starship’s reliability. Last December, it said on X that “SpaceX is committed to responsibly using airspace during launches and reentries, prioritizing public safety to protect people on the ground, at sea, and in the air.”
The FAA did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Disney, Royal Caribbean or Club Med.
Ron Madler, a professor of aerospace engineering at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, said the videos could help SpaceX “either confirm their breakup models or possibly to improve them.”
The mishap report for Flight 8, which rained debris near the Bahamas, said before that flight’s explosive failure, SpaceX did not have the proper “test stand” that was capable of testing the rocket’s engines “for a full Starship mission.” The remainder of the page was blacked out, so it was unclear from the report whether the company had found another way to fully test the engines before launch.
Flights 7 and 8 both involved the same model. Both ended in engine-related failures.
Text in the report around the statement about the test stand was redacted. But Jah said it “means some part of the engine’s actual flight behavior was being verified for the first time in flight rather than on the ground.”
John Crassidis, an aerospace engineering professor at the University at Buffalo, said launching before having a fully capable test stand was likely “a cost-saving decision.” In building rockets, he said, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has used both the old approach of launching and then fixing any issues that arise, and the newer approach of running simulations and ground tests first to head off problems.
“Doing too much of the old school can lead to too many mishaps and cost overruns,” he said. “Doing too much of the new school leads to long times to get things done and a reduction in flexibility.”

propublica.org.title: American Academy of Pediatrics Renews Call for Ban on Raw Milk
propublica.org.text:
The nation’s largest professional group of pediatricians has renewed its call for a nationwide ban on the sale and distribution of unpasteurized milk and other raw dairy products, according to a policy statement it published earlier this week.
The revised guidance from the American Academy of Pediatrics warns of the serious health risks from consuming raw dairy products, particularly for children, as well as pregnant and immunocompromised people.
“More and more people are discussing this as a potentially healthful thing to do, when in fact it’s a highly risky thing to do,” said the academy’s president, Dr. Andrew Racine. “So our responsibility, as the leading voice of pediatric healthcare in the United States that’s dedicated to the health and well-being of children, is to make sure that the accurate, evidence-based information is out there.”
The revised statement follows ProPublica reporting that dived deep into the causes and severe consequences of America’s current fascination with raw milk, which has not been heated to kill off harmful bacteria. Once limited to the fringes of health-food culture, unpasteurized milk has morphed into a widespread movement rooted in wellness trends and institutional distrust. Today, more than 10 million Americans drink it.
Most scientists and health experts agree that raw milk has no significant, proven nutritional benefits over its pasteurized counterpart and that it cannot treat or cure any disease. It also subjects its consumers to over 100 times the risk of foodborne illness, which can be especially dangerous for young children. Before milk pasteurization was widely adopted a century ago, thousands of children died each year from diseases linked to contaminated dairy.
As it has grown in popularity in recent years, raw dairy products have contributed to numerous outbreaks of pathogenic diseases, such as salmonella and E. coli. Over the past two years, nine states have experienced outbreaks that regulators have linked to raw dairy. Just last month, federal regulators linked an E. coli outbreak to unpasteurized cheese. Thirteen people fell ill, more than half of whom were young children.
As illnesses have surged, high-level lawmakers and government officials, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., have championed the industry instead of curbing it. In his federal role, Kennedy said he was “advocating” for raw milk and celebrated the release of a report to Make America Healthy Again with a toast of raw-milk shooters in the White House. The health department did not respond to ProPublica’s questions about the new professional guidance or the pediatric group’s call for a ban on raw milk sales.
Rep. Rosa DeLauro, a Connecticut Democrat who chairs the Congressional Food Safety Caucus, told ProPublica that she is taking the guidance of the academy “very seriously.”
“They see firsthand what these illnesses can do to children,” she said in an emailed statement. “Right now, Secretary of Health and Human Services RFK Jr. cannot even bring himself to tell parents not to give it to their kids.”
DeLauro said she was “supportive of any policy that reduces risk of exposure to harmful foods,” including putting warning labels on raw-milk products and maintaining adequate funding for outbreak prevention and tracking.
Federal law restricts the sale of raw milk across state lines, but states can decide how it can be sold within their boundaries. In recent years, proponents have fought to increase access to raw milk within states, often opposing efforts to limit its sales. People can legally purchase raw milk in all but a handful of states, either directly from a store or from a farmer, or even as “pet food.”
Last week, ProPublica detailed the case of two girls severely sickened last year after consuming raw goat milk from an unregulated farm in southern California. The state, which is teeming with black-market dairies, did little to punish the farmer who sold the families the milk. It allowed her to provide her own sample for testing, weeks after the outbreak began, and did not independently sample her grounds for traces of the pathogen, as state investigators have done in other cases. (The farmer told ProPublica that her milk, which tested negative for pathogens, did not cause the outbreak and claimed the families had knowingly bought milk that was not for human consumption, which they deny.)
The mother of one of the girls, a toddler who nearly died, had read about the purported benefits of unpasteurized milk on a site for the Raw Milk Institute, a nonprofit founded by Mark McAfee, one of the nation’s most prolific sellers. In a profile of the California farmer, ProPublica chronicled how social media influencers have amplified his claims and helped him build what is now a $30 million-a-year business even as regulators have linked it to more than a dozen recalls and outbreaks that have sickened hundreds. (McAfee previously defended the claims made on the institute’s website and maintained to ProPublica that raw milk still has therapeutic benefits.)
Members of the academy said they read and circulated ProPublica’s reporting as they drafted their statement.
“This product is being marketed to families as being beneficial for their kids,” said Dr. Adam Ratner, a pediatric infectious disease doctor in New York City and one of the lead authors of the academy’s revised statement. “They don’t see the risks, and unwittingly they end up making a decision that is much more dangerous.”
The academy first published a policy statement on raw milk in 2014, endorsing a nationwide ban on its sale and encouraging its members to reach out to state representatives to advocate for such a restriction. The statement published this week reaffirms this appeal with recent epidemiological evidence. In addition, it cites a growing concern of highly pathogenic avian influenza, which has been shown to contaminate unpasteurized milk.
Racine, the academy’s president, told ProPublica that the policy was also updated on account of “the rise in the discussion about the alleged benefits of raw milk and the fact that more people are experimenting with using it.”
“Prevention really is the best single way to keep children healthy and safe, and this is a preventive move,” he said. “The more that we can disseminate this information to a greater number of people, the healthier we’re going to be able to keep the children of this country.”

theintercept.com.title: ICE Agent on Scene of NYC Shooting Was Posing as Construction Worker, Eyewitness Says
theintercept.com.text:
U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents shot a person in New York City on Thursday afternoon, according to police.
The shooting took place around 4 p.m. in Manhattan’s Marble Hill neighborhood, according to a statement from the New York Police Department. The NYPD said the victim was taken to a local hospital and was conscious, but provided no further information about the victim.
Rep. Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y., told The Intercept that there was a child in the car and that the child is OK, which New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani later confirmed in a statement.
“This afternoon in Marble Hill, a New Yorker was shot by an ICE agent in a residential neighborhood. Early reports indicate agents surrounded him and a 5-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds,” Mamdani said. “We believe the child was physically unharmed.”
At a press conference, Espaillat said that he attempted to visit the shooting victim in the hospital, but was prevented from doing so by federal authorities.
“I went to the hospital to see the victim,” Espaillat said, “but we were not allowed by ICE agents to go in the room.”
A neighbor, Iris Rosa, said the shooting happened just as a nearby school was being let out. After hiding in a store for a few minutes, she said she went to look at the scene and said it looked like agents had shot into a car.
The victim, Rosa said, was on the ground bleeding and being held down by the agents. A baby, she said, was in the car and was held by ICE agents until someone picked the child up.
Photos of the aftermath of the shooting, taken by a neighbor and obtained by The Intercept, show apparent government agents in plain clothes and tactical vests pinning a man on the asphalt. Another man in a high-visibility vest is clutching an assault rifle while holding a phone between his cheek and shoulder.
Rosa, the neighbor, said a man with a high-visibility vest appeared to be posing as a construction worker, but as she watched, Rosa told The Intercept, the man took the vest and put it in a nearby vehicle.
ICE agents routinely pose as construction workers in order to stakeout targets for immigrations.
Representatives of Mayor Zohran Mamdani and ICE did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said the shooting occurred during “a targeted enforcement operation.”
“During the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon and the criminal illegal alien was injured,” the spokesperson wrote in a statement. “ICE officers immediately rendered aid. The individual is alive and at a local hospital. The FBI and HSI are on the scene. The incident remains under investigation.”
The victim is the latest of at least 25 people to be shot by federal immigration agents this year. In July, after two fatal ICE shootings and a botched arrest in Las Vegas by plainclothes agents wearing hooded sweatshirts, the agency mandated a new dress code for field operations.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she had been briefed on the shooting. “We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident,” she said on X.
“ICE’s violent tactics are a clear danger to all New Yorkers, as today’s shooting in a residential neighborhood demonstrates,” said Murad Awawdeh, the head of the advocacy group New York Immigration Coalition, in a statement. “This incident is another reminder of the unchecked, rampant violence ICE has been spreading throughout our communities.”

theintercept.com.title: Pete Hegseth’s Military of the Future: Defined by AI and an Utter Lack of Oversight
theintercept.com.text:
In his “state of the force” address last week, self-styled War Secretary Pete Hegseth coupled his usual attacks on the press, the Ivy League, and “beardos” and “weirdos” with new initiatives that have the potential to reshape the U.S. military for decades: an Autonomous Warfare Command, and an effort to map out the future of warfare called “Project Meridian.” The former, a combatant command devoted to AI-enabled robotic warfare, will have purchasing powers specifically designed to thwart effective oversight. The latter puts defense contractors, tech titans, and weapons merchants in charge of planning the military’s future — producing innumerable conflicts of interest.
The Pentagon has revealed few details about the command or the commission beyond barebones descriptions and Hegseth memorandums. The four-paragraph document that authorizes Project Meridian, for example, says little beyond a decree that the U.S. must “dominate” in “new domains, new ways of fighting” centered on “artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics, [and] biotechnology, among other critical high-tech areas.”
While billed as efforts to promote blue-sky thinking and catapult the Pentagon into the future, former defense officials as well as experts on government contracting say both initiatives are ripe for out-of-control spending as well as waste, fraud, and abuse.
One former official asked how Hegseth’s Pentagon would “plan for future wars when they didn’t plan for the current one,” referencing the failed war with Iran. A second former official foresaw tough sailing for both of Hegseth’s efforts due to institutional intransigence, inertia, and roadblocks that even Hegseth’s repeated purges of top brass would not help overcome.
I, Robot
AUTOWARCOM will be “a new four-star combatant command … built to scale autonomous and robotic capabilities across the joint force,” Hegseth said in a wide-ranging speech rife with Pentagon jargon and juvenile insults. The new command is scheduled to be formally established by October 1, 2027, according to a memo released following Hegseth’s speech at Marine Base Quantico, Virginia.
“The pace of war is changing faster than the processes to support it. Cheap computing, Super Intelligence, and advanced commercial manufacturing have enabled the proliferation of low-cost, high precision strike,” Hegseth explained, using President Donald Trump’s preferred and incorrect term for artificial intelligence before offering up a thunderstorm analogy. “We need bolts of lightning … our existing high-end kill chains,” he said, emphasizing the need for traditional and expensive weapons systems, like the Tomahawk missiles that leveled an elementary school in Minab, Iran. “We also need steady wind and rain: mass drones and other autonomous attritable systems that flip the cost exchange and impose unrelenting pressure on an adversary on the battlefield.”
A money pit in the making, according to the first former Pentagon official, AUTOWARCOM will — according to Hegseth — possess “directed manpower, budget, acquisition authorities and create dedicated military career pathways for Officers and Enlisted personnel.” Hegseth suggested weapons would be tested on battlefields whenever feasible. That former official, who spoke to The Intercept on the condition of anonymity due to his current employment, said to “expect a fiasco financially.”
This was echoed by Gabe Murphy, a policy analyst with Taxpayers for Common Sense. “By Secretary Hegseth’s own admission, the purpose of this combatant command is to cut out the oversight that autonomous systems so desperately need by deploying untested autonomous weapons in combat,” he told The Intercept. “That approach promises to waste a tremendous amount of taxpayer dollars while also endangering service members and threatening the missions they’re tasked with carrying out.”
Hegseth’s push for a command devoted to autonomous weapons comes amid a furious debate over safeguards for AI. The tech sector has been roiled by recent revelations that AI agents went rogue, circumvented controls and began colluding in secret; inserted “jailbreak-like instructions” into their own notes to free the models from human-imposed constraints; hacked or took aim at government websites, networks and databases around the world; and almost instigated a confrontation between the U.S. and China, both nuclear-armed powers. Questions also continue to mount over the AI-enabled Maven Smart System, built by Palantir and used by the military for targeting in Iran, that paved the way for the Minab strike that killed more than 150 people, most of them children.
Hegseth said he anticipated internal resistance within the military to the creation of AUTOWARCOM. Both former defense officials agreed it was a certainty.
Hegseth said that Owen West, who led the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit, and Max Strasiser, a Navy SEAL senior chief and a test pilot, will run the Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems (DRPM-UxS) “under a unique CEO-COO partnership.”
Their “culminating mission” will, said Hegseth, “take place over the course of months, clearing the path for Autonomous Warfare Command.” This will be conducted under a new moniker, Project Agincourt, a nod to a 1415 battle in which outnumbered English forces used longbows to defeat a larger French army, offered no quarter for a time during combat, and then massacred prisoners. (Hegseth has also advocated for offering no quarter to enemies, now a war crime.)
Project Agincourt will set up AUTOWARCOM while it simultaneously “prototype[s] a new construct called Warfighting Acquisition.” Hegseth laid out a move-fast-and-break-things vision for the new command. “This model fuses operators with entrepreneurs in rapid adaptation cycles, while distributing decisions and dollars closer to frontline units and the combatant commands,” he explained. “By removing unnecessary layers, reducing the distance between our warfighters and our world-leading innovators, and then giving the right people the authority to act — Project Agincourt will pilot innovation at the edge, in a way that only Americans can do.”
Both former officials said such an arrangement was likely to lead to both contracting fraud and technological failures.
(Armed) Conflicts of Interest
Hegseth also announced the formation of Project Meridian, an effort to study the future of warfare which he claimed would be “co-led by three of our nation’s best minds,” before clarifying that it would instead be run by Elon Musk, Newt Gingrich, and Palmer Luckey, the founder of the virtual reality firm Oculus Rift and defense contractor Anduril Industries. Assisted by War Department chief technology officer, Emil Michael, the three Trump boosters are tasked with ensuring “America’s long-term military superiority by identifying the capabilities required to achieve absolute technological dominance on the next-generation battlefield.” Hegseth said the project would be completed within 120 days, at which time the group would issue a final public report with a classified annex.
A Republican fundraising bundler partial to Hawaiian shirts and cargo shorts, Luckey fancies himself a techno-war futurist and believes tomorrow’s conflicts will be fought in a “subterranean domain,” with “weapons that move through the crust of the earth.” He says that “Anduril has working prototypes of subterranean systems that can deliver a variety of kinetic, electronic, and other effects.” Luckey also envisions the moon as a future battlespace. He said lunar warfare would resemble that of Robert Heinlein’s 1966 science fiction novel “The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress,” which includes subterranean combat and an electromagnetic catapult that lobs lunar boulders, with the kinetic force of atomic blasts, at the earth.
Anduril has been cleaning up on Pentagon contracts, inking a deal this year with the Army for commercial information technology potentially worth $20 billion. Anduril is also leading a contractor consortium, including the weapons-tech company Palantir — whose Maven Smart System contributed to the Minab school strike — helping build Trump’s “Golden Dome” missile defense system, which is predicted to be a trillion-dollar boondoggle.
Luckey joins Musk, whose firm SpaceX has been awarded billions for a key role in the Golden Dome project, as a defense contractor with a clear conflict of interest in mapping out the future of U.S. warfare. Musk, who donated more than a quarter of a billion dollars to getting Trump elected in 2024 and is providing at least $100 million to help Republican candidates during this election cycle, is returning to government service after flaming out last year as the head of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency. A cost-cutting agency that promised to save Americans trillions of dollars by eliminating waste, fraud, and abuse, DOGE failed to deliver on that promise, wasted taxpayer money, repeatedly misled the public about supposed savings, and may have played a role in hundreds of thousands of deaths.
“There is a genuine need for government reform and modernization, but we saw how Musk’s approach worked out with DOGE,” Murphy told The Intercept. “It failed spectacularly, creating disruptions, payouts for workers not working, firings and rehiring, and a pittance of the savings taxpayers were promised.”
Luckey and Musk will be joined at the helm of Project Meridian by the 83-year-old Gingrich, who resigned as House speaker in 1998 after admitting that he broke congressional rules and “brought down on the people’s house a controversy which could weaken the faith people have in their government.”
Hegseth announced that a meeting between “a small group” was to take place just after his Wednesday speech in a sensitive compartmented information facility at Quantico. Pentagon propaganda photos from the first meeting show 11 grim-looking men, including Musk, Gingrich, and Luckey, seated around a table as Hegseth holds forth.
The nonprofit MITRE Corporation, which conducts independent research for federal government agencies, announced that it will be coordinating Project Meridian and named 17 current board members beyond the Big Three, including Francis J. “Bing” West, a Vietnam War veteran, who served as the assistant secretary of defense for international security affairs under President Ronald Reagan from 1981 to 1983, and is the father of DRPM-UxS CEO Owen West; Rick Smith, the CEO of Axon, the manufacturer of Taser stun guns, which saw nine of 13 members of its ethics advisory board resign in 2022 over plans for a Taser-equipped drone project (which was then shelved); Joe Lonsdale, a co-founder of Palantir; and Safra Catz, former CEO of Oracle.
“Project Meridian is an unveiled effort to outsource our future military strategies to individuals and companies that stand to profit most from a hypermilitarized future,” said Murphy. “Their security solutions will predictably entail vast expenditures of taxpayer resources on unproven military systems that rely on the AI models and software these companies control.”
Hegseth’s office did not respond to questions about Project Meridian and AUTOWARCOM.
The New 1 Percent
Hegseth made the announcements of both AUTOWARCOM and Project Meridian in front of more than 500 junior officers and enlisted troops at the site where, a year before, he had ranted at generals about fitness and grooming standards, while promoting both Christianity and violence.
In this year’s diatribe, Hegseth touted his overhaul of the military, which has included firings of many top brass and an overwhelming emphasis on physical appearance, masculinity, and troops’ testosterone levels. “We are no longer the Woke Department or the Weak Department. Simple translation of that: No fatties. No trannies. No beardos. No weirdos. No wimps. No radicals,” Hegseth announced. “The ideological clowns are out. The patriotic cowboys are in — with testosterone testing on top.”
Despite laying out a future in which artificial, not human, intelligence will be ever more central to war-making, Hegseth ended his rant by nonetheless praising the troops, casting them as members of a violent and lethal warrior elite that are superior to civilians.
“See, the Ivy League faculty lounges, they’ll never understand you, and that’s OK, because they could never, ever do what you do. The media will mischaracterize you, and that’s OK. Because deep down they know you’re the real reason they live free. They envy you because you do real things every single day,” said Hegseth, an Ivy League-educated war chief who used to work for Fox News.
“You feel comfortable inside the violence. … Lethality is your calling card and victory your only acceptable end-state. The outside world can’t understand this, so stay true to this department. You don’t want to look like civilians, because you are different, you are set apart. You are warriors.” He added: “You are the real 1 percent.”

theintercept.com.title: Armed Border Agents Arrest Protesters, Bulldoze 200-Year-Old Tree to Build Border Wall
theintercept.com.text:
For more than 70 days, dozens of activists and an ancient cottonwood tree on the Arizona–Mexico border have successfully disrupted the construction of President Donald Trump’s ruinous $50 billion border wall.
Since July, one protester at a time has occupied the cottonwood, or the grandmother tree, as it is locally known. After three other cottonwoods in the area were torn down by government contractors, the remaining grandmother on the U.S. side of the border became the site of a growing protest camp in the remote town of Lochiel, Arizona, and neighboring Sonora, Mexico, where organizers gathered for more than a year to oppose the border wall’s construction.
On Monday, heavily armed federal agents moved in with force. Activists on the ground estimate that 150 Border Patrol officers — many of whom masked their faces — raided the encampment during the protesters’ morning prayer ceremony. At least 10 demonstrators were arrested, and the 200-year-old cottonwood was bulldozed.
As Arizona-based journalist John Washington reported, “agents began cutting the tree while a person was still sitting in its branches. Agents removed that person with a cherry picker and then felled the tree. Screams could be heard as ‘grandmother’ fell around 8:30 a.m.”
In the 48 hours since the early morning raid, land defenders have refused to leave and remain in an ongoing standoff with federal agents. Numerous participants told The Intercept that around 50 people are holding the line against further construction, with dozens more en route following urgent calls to support the encampment and defend the imperiled borderland ecology.
On Tuesday, another tree sitter climbed the last remaining cottonwood standing in the path of the border wall construction, this one on the Mexico side. The tree was briefly occupied by demonstrators in mid-August and, according to a press release from the land defenders, “is once again halting construction.”
The protesters’ aim to stop the construction of two parallel, 30-foot-high border walls ripping through the remote San Rafael Valley. Miles of the double wall structure have already been built in the area. The region is sparsely populated and hardly ever used as a border-crossing site by humans but is renowned as a unique wildlife migration corridor. The cottonwood felled on Monday was the last of four ancient grandmother trees on the Arizona side of the border, which stood in the path of planned wall construction.
Until this week, federal forces had left the encampment and tree sit in relative peace, largely, activists said, because the camp is located on private land. That fact had not changed on Monday.
“Border Patrol has been coming onto private property since yesterday morning. No warrants are shown,” Rachel, a land defender who withheld her last night out of concern for being targeted by law enforcement, said on a call with reporters on Tuesday. “There’s no legal ground for them to come onto private property. And the feeling is that they’re pushing through the construction process as quickly as possible, and they’ll deal with the consequences of the law later. They just want to push the wall through, regardless of the harm they have to cause to us and to the land in the process.”
According to Rachel and other activists on the ground who spoke to The Intercept, construction workers have moved quickly since the raid, digging a deep trench that threatens the roots of the newly occupied cottonwood on the Mexico side.
A statement on Monday from Belicia Lynch, a member of the De La Ossa family who owns one of the tracts of private property along the border, confirmed the protesters were welcome on her property. “I just want to thank you guys for being out there to not only protect the grandmother tree, but the land itself that many animals and bugs inhabit,” Lynch told the land defenders in the statement.
Border Patrol and the Department of Homeland Security have not yet responded to questions from The Intercept.
The federal attacks on the Lochiel encampment came on the heels of a legal victory for anti-border activists in Big Bend, Texas. On Friday, a U.S. district judge granted an injunction to stop all border wall construction in the Big Bend area, including in national and state parks, while the court hears a lawsuit brought by local environmental and community groups. In the order, the judge wrote that the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on at least one of their claims’ merits.
But with practically unlimited funding for his border regime, Trump’s administration can continue fueling money into his violent and destructive border wall. What activists in Lochiel, Sonora, Big Bend, and beyond make clear, however, is that the government’s victory cannot be assumed. Disruptions and interventions are not just possible but also an absolute necessity, and pressure can be applied in an array of directions.
As one Arizona-based Mexican American tree sit participant told The Intercept in August, “The border is everywhere, which means that there are subcontractors and there are power players maybe in your backyard, maybe in your city, maybe an hour drive from where you’re living.”
Rachel, the land defender, made the stakes of the fight clear.
“We have to stop this wall here because the trajectory they’re going on, there is no safety in the U.S. for anyone,” she said on Monday. The call was cut short as news spread through the encampment that federal agents would attempt to remove the tree sitter on the Mexico side. At the time of writing, the grandmother tree in Sonora remains occupied; the fight against Trump’s border wall, and all it represents, has not been lost.
In a social media post on Wednesday, encampment participants announced a “call to presence” to celebrate the life of the felled cottonwood and continue the anti-border struggle. “If you have been waiting to come to Lochiel, this is the time,” they said. “Let your heavy heart lead you to action!”

lemonde.fr/en.title: New York mayor will ask Trump to withdraw ICE after shooting
lemonde.fr/en.text:
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said, on Thursday, October 8, he would ask US President Donald Trump to remove federal immigration agents from the city as tensions flared over the latest shooting involving ICE.
The New York Police Department said a man had been shot around 4:00 pm in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx during an altercation with federal agents. Mamdani and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) later confirmed that the shooting occurred during an operation of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), the agency responsible for Trump's immigration crackdown.
A DHS spokesperson said in a statement that agents were attempting to "to arrest a criminal illegal alien from the Dominican Republic with a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny, and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs and weapons possession." It did not state how many officers fired their weapons or why.
"ICE officers immediately rendered aid. The individual is alive and at a local hospital," the DHS spokesperson said. The department initially claimed that the person targeted had associations with a Dominican gang, but later issued a revised statement removing that sentence.
Mamdani said that a 5-year-old child was in the car when the altercation occurred. "This is an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation," the Democratic mayor said on X, adding that he had called the president. "When we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities," he added.
Trump, a Republican, heavily criticized Mamdani before he took office in January, but the two men have since struck a surprisingly warm relationship.
Several hundred protesters gathered peacefully at the scene of the shooting on Thursday evening to express opposition to Trump's crackdown, Agence France-Presse (AFP) observed. Many people then moved to the nearby hospital where the victim was being treated.
Tensions with the police escalated when some protesters attempted to prevent cars from leaving the hospital, before being moved away from the entrance by law enforcement, who set up barriers.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted on X on Thursday, saying she expects "federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident."
"This incident is another reminder of the unchecked, rampant violence ICE has been spreading throughout our communities," said Murad Awawdeh, president of the New York Immigration Coalition. "We demand an immediate investigation into the shooting, the release of the body camera footage and accountability for any ICE agents who used excessive force."
ICE has been involved in several high-profile shootings this year, including the killing of two US citizens in Minneapolis, which sparked angry protests.
New York, a Democratic stronghold, is one of several US cities that bars its police force from assisting with federal immigration enforcement.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Between record debt and high school protests, France's situation draws global attention
lemonde.fr/en.text:
France is accustomed to international media exposure, with its social protest movements earning a certain reputation. Yet the high school protest movement has attracted especially strong coverage, set against the backdrop of a debt crisis that has alarmed many. The movement's youthful, diverse, social media-driven and, at times, violent nature has caught the media's interest, while also fueling xenophobic rhetoric among leaders of the international far right.
In the United States, where France rarely grabs attention and media generally focus on domestic affairs, the country has become a major topic of conversation. Tensions over debt have dominated economic headlines and sparked extensive commentary on Wall Street, which sees France as proof of the failure of a country addicted to government spending. Meanwhile, the protests have propelled figures from the radical left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) party into the spotlight, such as the mayor of the Parisian suburb Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, who has given interviews as far afield as CNN. Footage of the riots has also circulated widely on far-right MAGA social media channels.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Paris officials seek to reduce the area under heritage protection in the capital
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Paris officials are aiming to undo two decisions regarding heritage protection in the city, taken during the final months of Anne Hidalgo's term as mayor (2014-2026), and to restore proper order to the process. This was the rationale put forward by the new Socialist-Green-Communist majority, as it asked the Council of Paris during meetings from October 6 to 9 to annul two resolutions adopted in June and November 2025 regarding the creation of a "Remarkable Heritage Site" (site patrimonial remarquable). Its intends to reconsider the boundaries of this zone, which it now considers overly broad.
On Wednesday, October 7, the right immediately denounced what it called "a real step backwards" and warned of a "lack of protection" for Paris's heritage, arguing that this system enables "the reconciliation of the city's evolution with adaptation to climate change."
It was precisely because they believed the opposite that Paris's new Socialist mayor, Emmanuel Grégoire, and his majority insisted on reopening the debate, even though the process was already well underway. At the heart of the discussions was a crucial question: Is it the city of Paris or the French state that has the final say over the buildings and landscape of the capital? The answer carries a double challenge: preserving these assets, but also ensuring their necessary – and urgent – adaptation to climate change, as the summer of 2026 so starkly reminded everyone.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Lutetia wall: 'An archeological discovery can be instantaneous, but knowledge never is'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
The Lutetia wall is everywhere. Barely uncovered beneath the Hôtel-Dieu in Paris, it was quickly dubbed "the Gallic rampart" in the press release issued on September 23 by the French Ministry of Culture. The remains are remarkable, and the hypothesis is serious. However, its precise function, chronology and the circumstances of its abandonment have yet to be determined. The City of Paris emphasized that further research could supplement initial interpretations, "or even refute them."
That has not stopped the wall from beginning a second life. Broadcast far and wide, it has already transported us back to the Parisii people, to Caesar, to Vercingetorix, and to the origins of Paris. The wall has yet to reveal its full story, but it is already being tasked with telling ours.
The problem is neither the excavation itself nor the significance of the find. It is the process that almost instantly transforms an archeological fact into a historical event, as if these remains, now seen as "stones of truth," could speak for themselves. By wanting to make the stones speak before we have even questioned them, does archeology risk reverting to a kind of divination?
The Lutetia wall highlights the need to distinguish between two forms of archeology, both legitimate, but with different objectives. The first is heritage archeology. It identifies, documents, protects, preserves and transmits the remains of the past. Its social function is essential, and this is the most visible form of archeology: a rampart, a tomb, a palace, or a treasure can easily be shown, narrated and publicized.
But there is another archeology, one that is fully part of the humanities. It is defined not by the age or heritage value of its objects, but by a question: What can we understand about human beings from the material traces of their actions? Archeology, in this sense, is truly an art of investigation. The excavation is the initial scene, almost like a crime scene, where every detail must be recorded because even the smallest clue can be significant.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Gaza rescuers say Israeli fire kills seven
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Gaza's civil defense rescue service said, on Thursday, October 8, that seven people were killed in separate Israeli strikes throughout the day, while the Israeli army said three of the victims were "military operatives." Six of the seven were killed in various parts of Gaza City. Two people were killed in a drone strike on a car, while one was killed in a drone attack on a tent in an encampment for displaced people, the rescue service and al-Shifa hospital said.
The Israeli army told Agence France-Presse (AFP) that the three targeted were "military operatives in terrorist organizations."
The civil defense said, "Two people, a woman and a child, were killed and others were wounded when Israeli aircraft bombed a residential building" in Gaza City, adding that "one person was killed by Israeli fire southeast of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza."
A woman was also killed by artillery shelling in Gaza City, health officials reported. Contacted by AFP, the Israeli army said it was checking the reports about the other four victims.
Hamas on Thursday denied Israeli claims that it uses Gaza hospitals for military activities, after the army said Wednesday that militants "advanced attacks from within (Kamal Adwan) hospital" in northern Gaza. Hamas, in a statement, called the accusations "criminal incitement."
Israel's military offensive against the Islamist group has displaced nearly all the population of Gaza and killed more than 74,200 people, according to Gaza's health ministry, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations. They do not distinguish between militants and civilians.
The war began after Hamas launched an unprecedented attack against Israel on October 7, 2023. Since a ceasefire was declared in October last year, Israeli forces have killed at least 1,450 people in Gaza, according to the ministry. The Israeli military has declared the deaths of five soldiers and one civilian contractor in the same period.

lemonde.fr/en.title: 'Trump dividend': Can promising voters a check help win an election?
lemonde.fr/en.text:
Trailing in the polls, Donald Trump believes he has found a winning formula to turn public opinion around and limit electoral losses in the November 3 elections for the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate. Since September 10, he has been promising to give "all adult citizens in the United States of America" a $5,000 check (about €4,400) if the Republicans manage to keep control of both chambers. He is calling it, unsurprisingly, the "Trump Dividend."
The corrupt pact being offered to voters is not illegal. After all, such campaign promises funded by taxpayers are as old as elections themselves: "Every election is sort of an advance auction sale of stolen goods," as American journalist HL Mencken (1880-1956) wryly put it. But Trump's announcement shocked many, both ethically and in terms of budget. If paid out, the Trump Dividend would increase the already massive US public debt by $1.25 trillion.
To be clear, the chances of these $5,000 checks actually landing in the pockets of 250 million adult citizens are slim. Republicans may hope to retain the Senate, but they hold a narrow majority (218 seats out of 435) in the House of Representatives, which is very likely to swing to the Democrats. Nevertheless, the Trump Dividend could have a significant electoral impact. Voters do not cast their ballots solely for values or ideas: They do not forget their material interests.
Clear and credible
Several economists have documented the impact of such promises. In 2017, Italian researcher Matteo Alpino, then at the University of Oslo, published a rigorous study on a pledge made by Silvio Berlusconi (1936-2023) at the very end of his 2006 campaign in Italy. At the time, Berlusconi was president of the Council of Ministers and facing the moderate left leader, Romano Prodi. During their final televised debate, Berlusconi made a surprise announcement: He vowed to scrap the property tax on primary residences, in the name of "sacrosanct respect for the family home" – a promise worth €3 billion.

lemonde.fr/en.title: High school protests draw tens of thousands across France for second time in a week
lemonde.fr/en.text:
The students wanted to "take the Bastille." So they filled this symbolic square in central Paris to the brim, determined to keep up a movement that shows no sign of slowing. As in previous demonstrations two days prior, tens of thousands of high school and university students turned out to demand better learning conditions and to protest against the far-right Rassemblement National (RN) party and police violence. On Thursday, October 8, marches drew 71,500 people nationwide, including 24,500 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry. In addition, 55,000 young people took part in protests outside schools, with only some joining the larger gatherings.
"Act IV" began Thursday morning in Lyon, where around 3,500 people – high school and university students and teachers – marched from Bron in the greater Lyon area to the 8th arrondissement, with no reported incidents. Among them was a local mother of Algerian origin, in tears: "When I see all these police officers, I'm scared, I'm scared for our children," she said. "I come from a country where young people have no right to protest."
Particularly fired up, students from Lyon-II and Lyon-III universities led the march. "We send you SOS, you send us your riot police," read the sign carried by Oriane (those identified by first name only did not want to give their surnames), a psychology student at Lyon-II. Brief clashes broke out after the official protest dispersed.
In Marseille, too, university students like Amira and Bradley turned out in force. "We were already here on Tuesday and were tear-gassed by the riot police. We're shocked to see high school students left with lifelong injuries just for protesting," explained Amira, who graduated from high school only two years ago. Their University Institute of Technology in northern Marseille was closed and evacuated that morning. "There's private security at the entrance… It's just to scare us," Amira complained. "We're very dissatisfied with the answers we've been given. In class, any discussion is banned. That's also why we're here. To make ourselves heard," added Bradley.

lemonde.fr/en.title: Pentagon chief says execution of military base shooter to be 'public'
lemonde.fr/en.text:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the firing squad execution of convicted military base shooter Nidal Hasan will be "public," according to a video shared Thursday, October 8, by the Pentagon.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist, shot dead 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009. His execution will be the first by the US military since 1961, and the first it has carried out by firing squad since World War II.
"He's going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth told right-wing influencer Jack Posobiec in a clip posted on X by various official Pentagon accounts. "People need to understand that (...) there's serious consequence for these types of things," Hegseth said, speaking aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier.
Hegseth noted that it would be the military's first firing squad execution since the Second World War – a reference to the case of Eddie Slovik, who was put to death for desertion in 1945. "I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was win, which was understand when the enemy attacks you, you need to stand your ground," Hegseth said.
In a separate clip, Posobiec asked the Pentagon chief if Hasan had made any final request. "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3," Hegseth said – the day Hasan is slated to die.
The Pentagon announced earlier this week that US President Donald Trump had approved Hasan's execution for the 2009 fatal shooting 13 people at Fort Hood. Twelve of the dead and 30 of the wounded were soldiers. Hasan was shot and partially paralyzed by a civilian police officer who responded to the attack. He was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 for carrying out the Al-Qaeda inspired attack.
The court that convicted Hasan was told that he was opposed to the US military's occupations of Iraq and Afghanistan, and that he had spoken online with an alleged Al-Qaeda figure, radical cleric Anwar al-Awlaki, an American citizen subsequently killed in a US drone strike in Yemen.
The last US military execution was carried out in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder.
The Death Penalty Information Center says that 135 soldiers have been executed by the US military since 1916.
According to rights group Amnesty International, at least 17 public executions are known to have been carried out last year – six in Afghanistan and 11 in Iran.

lemonde.fr/en.title: France struggles to reassure financial markets as Asian investors fuel distrust
lemonde.fr/en.text:
French Economy Minister Roland Lescure is no stranger to "roadshows," having spent many years in the banking sector. Now he is back on the road defending France to institutional investors in major global financial centers. On Thursday, October 8, he gathered about a dozen international banks and asset managers in London to reassure them about France's financial outlook and its ability to pass the 2027 budget, if necessary, by executive order.
The day before, he gave an interview to the Wall Street Journal to deliver the same message to American investors. "We're going to use whatever it takes," the French minister pledged, hoping that this oft-repeated phrase would bring the same relief as when Mario Draghi rescued the euro on July 26, 2012.
Lescure will then travel to Luxembourg on Friday. While the ECOFIN Council, which brings together the economy ministers of the 27 European Union countries, may officially be devoted to the capital markets union, it will primarily allow him to discuss with his counterparts the best way to ease bond market tensions, even though any intervention by the European Central Bank (ECB) is entirely ruled out at this stage. Finally, the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings in Bangkok, which begin on Sunday, will give him the opportunity to hold numerous one-on-one discussions with global financial players, including certain Asian funds that are already turning away from France.
